Transcript:

Every superpower on Earth died at the same time. And no one has ever been able to say who killed them.

In a single lifetime, the mightiest kingdoms of the ancient world all fell at once. Not one of them. All of them.

Mycenaean Greece. The mighty Hittite Empire. The rich trading cities of the coast. Wiped off the map inside about fifty

years. And then something happened that still doesn't feel real. The few who survived were so broken they forgot how to write. A whole civilization lost its script. And it stayed that way for roughly

three hundred years. The thing I keep circling is that no single blow did this. It was how each disaster handed the next one a

loaded gun. So here is the question that has haunted historians for thirty centuries. What force is strong enough to kill every superpower on the planet at once? Because there is a lineup of suspects.

And there is no confession. This is the greatest cold case in human history, and I am going to walk you through the suspects one by one. Fair warning. It gets worse with every single one. Start with how strong this

world was. That is the first trap. This was not a collection of isolated tribes. This was a globalized world. Egypt, the Hittites, the Greeks, Babylon, Cyprus, the kings of the coast, all linked together.

They wrote each other letters. They married each other's daughters. They shipped copper and tin and gold across the entire known sea.

We even found the proof at the bottom of the ocean. A single wooden ship that sank off the coast of Turkey. Divers pulled up ten tons of copper. A ton of tin.

Treasure from Egypt, from the Levant, from Mesopotamia, from Greece. One boat carrying a whole world in its belly. And here is the fuse nobody

sees at first. Bronze is the metal that named this entire age. But bronze is an alloy. You need copper, and you need tin.

And the tin had to be carried from far, far away, across the whole trade network. Which means the strongest empires on Earth were all standing on the same thread. Cut that thread, and every one

of them falls together. They were not just connected. They were fragile. Now cut the first thread.

The sky turns against them. Around twelve hundred BC, a drought settles over the entire eastern Mediterranean. Not a bad summer. A mega-drought. We can read it in the pollen buried in ancient lake beds.

By some estimates it lasted a hundred and fifty years. In some places, closer to three hundred. The rivers shrink. The Nile floods weaken.

The rain simply stops coming. And a world of millions of people is suddenly staring at empty fields. But drought is only the first suspect. Because a dry field leads to something far more frightening.

People start to starve. This is where the letters get desperate. And here is a detail I still can't shake. When the famine bit, the great kings did not go to war over the last of the grain. They shipped it to each other.

Egypt sent grain north to the Hittites, and a pharaoh wrote that it was sent to keep the land of Hatti alive. Keeping your rival breathing, because if he falls,

you might be next. Then it gets darker. A Hittite king writes to a coastal city with a demand that reads like a scream. He needs a ship. He needs a crew. He needs roughly four hundred and fifty tons of grain. And he calls it, in his own words, a matter of life or death.

Read that again. The empire that once terrified Egypt is now begging a smaller kingdom for food. And here is the cruel part.

Their whole economy ran through the palace. Everything flowed in, everything flowed out, all controlled from the top. It was efficient. It was rich. And it had absolutely no backup plan.

When the center couldn't feed people, there was nothing underneath to catch them. So now you have drought. And famine.

Two suspects in the room. You would think that is enough to explain a collapse. It isn't. Because the ground itself is about to betray them.

Some scientists believe the region was hit by what they call an earthquake storm. Not one quake. A rapid-fire sequence of them, rolling across the land over about fifty years, from Greece all the way to Anatolia.

You can still see the damage in the stones at Mycenae. At Tiryns. Great walls cracked and toppled.

And watch what the survivors do next. They start building differently. Massive walls of enormous boulders. Heavy fortified gates. These people were suddenly afraid. Not just of the earth shaking.

Of what might be coming for them. Now, I have to be honest with you here, the way the historians are honest. The earthquake storm is a theory, and a debated one. Some scholars doubt a quake brought Mycenae down.

That is the strange thing about this whole mystery. Every suspect has an alibi. No single one of them can be pinned with the crime. Which brings us to

the suspect everyone loves to blame. The ships appear on the horizon. Out of the sea come raiders. The Egyptians called them, roughly, the peoples of the sea. And for a long time, this was the answer.

A mysterious horde of invaders who burned the Bronze Age to the ground. Case closed. But wait. Who were they, actually?

Nobody knows for sure. That is the honest, haunting truth. Line them up like a suspect row. The Peleset. The Sherden. The Shekelesh. The Denyen. Strange names carved on Egyptian stone, and next to each one, a shrug.

We are not even sure which came from Sicily, which from the islands of Greece, which from somewhere we have never even found. Their true home, their real identity, whether they were one people at all, remains a genuine mystery to this day.

And here is the part almost nobody tells you about the Sea Peoples. They may not have been an invading army so much as a fleeing one.

Think about it. A drought. A famine. Whole populations with nowhere left to farm, piling into boats, moving along the coast in search of anywhere that still had food. They weren't only causing the collapse.

They were running from it. Refugees and raiders at the same time. The victim and the weapon. Now watch the dominoes actually fall.

We have the last words of a dying city. A coastal kingdom called Ugarit. Its final letters were dug out of the ruins, and they are chilling.

The king writes that the enemy's ships have already come. That his cities are burned. That they have done terrible things in his land. Then the letters stop. Ugarit burned to the ground and was never lived in again.

And here is the ghost detail. Those clay tablets survived for one reason only. The fire that destroyed the city baked the clay hard as stone. We can read his last cry for help today because the disaster that killed him preserved it. His scream, fossilized by the flames.

The Hittite capital falls next, and not the way you would expect. There was no glorious last stand at Hattusa. The diggers found something eerier.

The people had already left. The royal family, the scribes, the treasures, all gone before the end. They evacuated their own capital and walked away. And then the empty city was burned. A ghost town set on fire.

Only Egypt holds the line. A pharaoh named Ramesses the Third meets the Sea Peoples in a huge land-and-sea battle in the Nile Delta.

His temple walls scream that he won, that he killed enemies by the thousands. Maybe he did. The numbers are royal propaganda, so we take them with caution.

But even in winning, Egypt was gutted. It survived the storm and never fully stood tall again. And here is the clue that breaks

the easy answer for good. Kingdoms far from any coast fell too. Deep inland, the ancient dynasty that ruled Babylon toppled as well. Even Troy, the city of legend, burned in roughly this same dark window.

No fleet of raiders could have reached them all. Something bigger than any army was loose in the world. This is the moment historians call a systems collapse.

One severed trade route starves the next kingdom. That kingdom falls, and its collapse drags down the next. Cut one thread, and the whole web unravels, faster and faster, until there is almost nothing left to fall. And what is left is the sound

that gives this whole story its horror. Silence. The palaces are ash. The kings are gone. The trade ships stop sailing. And in Greece, the

writing simply ends. The script they used, called Linear B, vanishes completely. Because it only ever recorded the palace accounts, and when the palaces died, there was no reason left to write at all. Sit with that.

A literate world went dark. By some estimates, as many as nine out of ten small settlements in southern Greece were simply abandoned. The cities emptied. The population crashed.

And for roughly three hundred years, Greece could not read or write a single word. When writing finally returned, it was not even the same system.

It was a brand new alphabet, borrowed from elsewhere. The old script was gone forever. Every hero, every king, every song from before the dark, unwritten and unremembered. They didn't just lose a civilization.

They lost its memory of itself. So who did it? Who killed every superpower on Earth at once?

Here is the answer, and it is the reason this story genuinely frightens the people who study it. Nobody did. And everybody did. There is no single villain.

The drought weakened them, so the famine could bite. The famine drove the migrations, so the raiders came. The earthquakes shattered the cities that were already starving. The trade collapsed, so the kingdoms that depended on it fell in a row.

Each disaster made the next one deadlier. A perfect storm, with no one hand to blame. And that is the terror of it. A whole civilized world can die with no single killer to point at. Not conquered. Not cursed.

Just overwhelmed, all at once, by everything. And notice, it was not the whole planet that fell. It was the connected part. The web of palaces that all leaned on each other. We like to think we have outgrown

that danger. We are more connected than any Bronze Age king ever dreamed. So was the world that shipped its tin across the sea, right up until the thread snapped.

That is the warning I take from it. Collapse rarely arrives as one big thing. It comes as everything at once, a little too late to stop.

Remember how we started. A connected world, vanishing in a lifetime. A people who forgot how to write. Three thousand years later, we are

still reading the last letter of a doomed king, only because the fire that killed him saved his final words. That is the whole Bronze Age in one image. A scream, baked into clay, waiting in the dark for someone to finally hear it. Out of that silence, eventually,

new peoples rose. New tools. A new alphabet, the ancestor of the very letters on your screen right now. But that is a different story.

Next time, we crown a very different kind of power. One that would build its entire world around never being caught weak and starving like this again. We are going to Sparta.

Subscribe, and stay with me, because the empires that clawed their way out of these ashes are somehow even stranger than the world that burned.

## Mansa Musa: The Richest Man Ever Began as a Boy Who Couldn't Walk

URL: https://doodlehistory.com/episodes/mali/
Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HGK8SAJoyUg

The Mali Empire made Mansa Musa, by most reckonings the richest human who ever lived — but it began with Sundiata Keita, a prince who, by legend, was born unable to walk. This is the true story of medieval West Africa's golden empire: the mocked, exiled boy who founded it, the trans-Saharan gold that made its king famous as far away as Europe, and how the whole thing quietly faded.

The Mali Empire explained, from Sundiata Keita and the Battle of Kirina to Mansa Musa's staggering 1324 pilgrimage to Mecca. How did the trans-Saharan gold and salt trade make medieval Mali one of the richest empires in history? Why did Mansa Musa's gold crash the price of gold in Egypt? How did Timbuktu grow into a legendary center of Islamic learning — and how did the Mali Empire fall to the rising Songhai? The full history of medieval West Africa: Sundiata, Mansa Musa, Timbuktu, and the gold that helped fund the medieval world. A history of medieval African civilization: the armies and battles that built the empire, the trans-Saharan trade that funded it, and the manuscripts of Timbuktu that preserved its scholarship.

Every "richest people in history" list has the same name on top.

Above the oil barons. Above the tech billionaires.

Above Musk. Above Bezos. And it does not belong to any of them.

It belongs to a medieval African king. A man whose empire began, by

its own legend, with a boy who could not walk. A prince mocked for his legs. Driven into exile as a child.

So how does a boy in the dirt end up founding the richest empire of its age?

It starts with iron braces. And a boy who refused to stay down.

And here is what gets me about this story. We remember Mali for one man's gold.

But its real fortune was never the gold at all. It was a boy everyone had written off,

deciding to stand up. The king on top of that list was named Mansa Musa. And we will get to his gold. All of it. But his empire did not

begin with him. It began, a hundred years before him, with that boy in the dirt. So we leave the gold behind for now, and we go looking for

the boy. West Africa, near the southern edge of the Sahara.

The land of the Mande people. This is where the griots come in. For seven hundred years, West African bards have carried one story by

memory alone. Singing it. Father to son. It is called the Epic of Sundiata. And as the epic tells it, this is

how Mali was born. A prince is born to the Keita clan, around the year

twelve ten. His name is Sundiata. It means something close to "the hungering lion."

But this lion cannot stand. As a small child, the story goes,

his legs will not hold him. The children laugh.

The court whispers that he is cursed. And when his father dies, Sundiata

and his mother are pushed aside. Then driven into exile.

Here is the boy who will one day build an empire of gold. Face down in the dirt. With nothing. But the epic gives us one unforgettable

moment. One day, the boy decides he will rise.

They fit iron braces to his legs. He grips them, and he pulls.

Slowly, painfully, Sundiata stands. He takes one step.

Then another. The boy who could not walk is now the tallest figure in the room.

Hold onto that image. We are going to need it. While Sundiata grows up in

exile, his homeland falls to a tyrant. His name is Sumanguru, king of the

Sosso. In the epic, he is more than a king. He is a cruel

sorcerer. One by one, he crushes the Mande clans.

And the beaten people start to ask a question. Where is the exiled prince?

Because Sundiata has not been idle. In exile, he has grown into a warrior. The scattered clans send for him. Come home.

Fight for us. So he comes home. Around the year twelve thirty-five, two armies

meet on a plain called Kirina. The boy they called cursed, against

the sorcerer-king. As the epic tells it, it was a duel of sorcery as much

as steel. And Sundiata won it. Sumanguru's power breaks.

His army breaks with it. And on that field, the Mali Empire is born.

But Sundiata does something far rarer than winning a battle.

He gathers the clans on an open plain and gives them a charter.

It is called the Kurukan Fuga. A spoken constitution.

A code of laws binding every clan into one people.

Seven centuries later, UNESCO would honor it as one of the world's earliest declarations

of rights. And Sundiata takes a new title.

Mansa. King. Master. The boy they mocked is now the first Mansa of Mali.

That is the flip. But a title is not a fortune. So where does all the gold actually come from? The answer is in the

ground. And in the desert. Mali sat on top of gold. The goldfields of Bambuk and Bure held some of the richest deposits in the medieval

world. But gold alone cannot feed an empire.

You cannot eat it. And out in the Sahara, the truly precious thing was not

gold. It was salt. Salt to survive the heat. Salt to keep food from spoiling. In desert mines like Taghaza, workers cut salt into great slabs and loaded them onto camels.

Gold came up from the south. Salt came down from the north. And right in the middle sat Mali, taking a cut of everything.

By some accounts, out there, salt was worth almost its weight in gold.

Gram for gram. West Africa supplied a huge share of the medieval Mediterranean's gold. The coins of Venice, of Genoa, of Cairo were

minted from it. And Mali's rulers took their money three ways at once.

They taxed every load that crossed their land.

They traded gold on their own account. And they controlled the mines on top of that.

Three rivers of gold, all flowing to one throne. This is the machine that made a mansa the richest man alive.

And around the year thirteen twelve, that machine passed to one particular king. His name was Musa. His rise to the throne is itself

a legend. The story Musa himself told in Cairo went like this.

The king before him did not die. He sailed away. He was obsessed with one question. What lies beyond the far edge of the ocean?

So, the legend says, he launched a great fleet west into the open Atlantic,

chasing the far shore. He was never seen again.

And the richest throne on Earth fell to Musa. Careful, though. This is only a story Musa told. There is no proof any fleet ever crossed that ocean. It is legend, not history. But the man it left in charge was very

real. And in thirteen twenty-four, Mansa Musa set out on the pilgrimage to Mecca. He did not travel quietly.

According to Arab chroniclers, his caravan numbered around sixty thousand people.

By their accounts, twelve thousand servants walked in silk and brocade.

Five hundred men went ahead of him, each carrying a staff of solid

gold. And behind them, by some accounts, a hundred camels, each hauling hundreds of pounds of gold. Picture that line stretching across the desert.

A moving city of gold. And in Cairo, something finally breaks.

Musa arrives, and he spends. He gives. He hands the sultan of Egypt a fortune

in gold just to say hello. Camel-loads of it, pressed on beggars

and merchants, on anyone who bows. He gives away so much that

the price of gold across Egypt collapses. Not for a week. Not for a month. By one Cairo scholar's account, it stayed low for about twelve years. One man. One visit. And a whole region's economy tips

over. Remember that name at the top of every "richest ever" list?

This is why it is there. So how rich was he, really? Honestly, no one can say. Modern lists love to slap a number

on it. Four hundred billion dollars, some claim.

But the honest answer is wilder. His wealth cannot really be counted. So rich the number simply breaks. And Musa did not just spend the gold.

He used it. He came home and turned a trading town on the Niger River

into a jewel of the world. Timbuktu.

By one account, he hired an architect from far-off Granada and paid him in

gold. Under Musa, Timbuktu raised the great Djinguereber mosque,

built of mud brick and wood, finished around thirteen thirty.

And its Sankore mosque grew into a famed center of Islamic learning, drawing

scholars from across the Muslim world. Then, in thirteen seventy-five, something

remarkable happened far away in Europe. Mapmakers in Spain drew

a grand new map of the known world. And in the middle of West Africa, they

drew a single king. Crowned in gold. Holding up a huge nugget of it. The caption called him the richest, noblest king of that land.

Europe had never met Mansa Musa. But Europe had heard of his gold.

And it put him on the map. Here is the part nobody tells you about Musa's empire.

It was not just rich. It actually worked. A few decades later, a

man arrived who had seen the world. His name was Ibn Battuta. A traveler from Morocco. By the time he reached Mali, around thirteen fifty-two, he had crossed most of the known world. Hard to impress.

Mali impressed him. What amazed him first was not the gold. It was the safety. He wrote that neither traveler nor local had

anything to fear from thief or robber. One of the largest empires

of its day. Millions of people. And a stranger could cross it, carrying

gold, and arrive safe. He watched a court drowning in ceremony.

Officials with gold-hilted swords and quivers of gold and silver.

Subjects who threw themselves to the ground before the mansa and poured dust on

their own heads to show respect. He admired how seriously Mali took

justice, and its faith. He noted that some parents would put a child in chains until the boy had memorized the Quran. Some of it he found strange.

Some of it he found excessive. But the verdict, from a man who had seen almost everything? This was one of the best-ordered kingdoms on Earth.

An empire like that feels like it should last forever. It did not. Every empire has one weakness that gold cannot fix. Who rules next.

Mali's golden age ran on strong kings. Musa. Then his brother, Mansa Suleyman, the last of the great ones.

Ibn Battuta actually met Suleyman and found him a bit of a miser next to Musa.

But he held the empire together. And then, around thirteen

sixty, Suleyman died. And the strong hand was gone. What came next is

the thing that kills empires from the inside. Succession. Son against nephew. Cousin against cousin.

A run of short, contested reigns, each one weaker than the last.

While the center fought itself, the edges pulled away.

Around fourteen hundred, the city of Gao broke free.

And Gao was home to a rising people. The Songhai.

The empire Mali once ruled was about to become the empire that replaced

it. Then the desert came for the crown jewel. Around fourteen thirty-three, Tuareg raiders swept in from the Sahara

and seized Timbuktu itself. The city of gold and books slipped out of

Mali's hands. Then came the man who finished it.

Sunni Ali of Songhai. He drove the Tuareg from Timbuktu, took the trading cities, and made Songhai the master of the Niger. Everything Mali had built, Songhai now held.

Mali did not die in one dramatic fall. It faded. It shrank back to the small heartland where Sundiata had started.

A rump kingdom, remembering when it was the richest place on Earth. By the sixteen hundreds, it was gone. So what is left of an empire that

faded five hundred years ago? Far more than you would think. Start with Timbuktu. The city outlived the empire.

And so did its books. Thousands of medieval manuscripts survived there. Science, law, poetry, astronomy, all written by hand.

And here is the part that will surprise you. In twenty twelve, when

armed extremists seized Timbuktu, its people refused to let

the books burn. Ordinary librarians smuggled the manuscripts out. In trunks. In rice sacks. Down the river, to safety. Seven hundred years on, they were still guarding the empire's mind.

And the story of Sundiata? It never needed writing to survive.

The griots are still singing it. In West Africa today, you

can hear the Epic of Sundiata performed. The same story.

Carried by voice across seven centuries. The boy who could not walk still stands

up, every single time it is told. And Mansa Musa? He is more famous now than he has been in six hundred years.

His name is back at the top of those "richest ever" lists.

In classrooms. In video games. The man who crashed the price of gold is viral all over again. Here is what it all comes down to.

We started with a name at the top of every "richest ever" list.

But the empire beneath that name did not begin with gold.

It began with a boy on the ground, who gripped two iron braces and decided to stand.

That was the real fortune. Not the gold. The rising.

That is the part I want you to keep. The gold is only ever what the rising paid for. Not the fortune. The boy who decided to stand.

So the next time that "richest ever" list scrolls past you, you will know where the story

really starts. But the next story we tell is not a rise.

It is an ending. Next time: the Bronze Age Collapse. The catastrophe that history still cannot explain.

Subscribe, so you are there when it happens.

## The Trojan Horse Isn’t in the Iliad. So Was the Trojan War Even Real?

URL: https://doodlehistory.com/episodes/trojan-war/
Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=KpJtzLKbwzc
Published: 2026-09-10 · Length: 13 min

The Trojan War is the most famous story in history that nobody could prove. So we went through it claim by claim and ruled on each one: the wooden horse, the thousand ships, the ten-year siege, Priam's gold, and the city itself. Some of it collapses the moment you touch it. One piece survives in a place nobody was even looking.

Did the Trojan War really happen? This is the Trojan War explained as a verdict rather than a retelling: how much of Homer's Iliad is history, how much is myth, and what archaeology at the mound of Hisarlik in north-west Turkey can and cannot prove. We cover why the Trojan horse is not in the Iliad at all, why the face that launched a thousand ships is Christopher Marlowe and not Homer, why Frank Calvert and not Heinrich Schliemann worked out where Troy was, why Priam's Treasure came from the wrong city by roughly a thousand years, why Bronze Age Troy was Anatolian rather than Greek, what the burn layer of Troy VIIa actually shows, and what the Hittite clay tablets from Hattusa say about a city called Wilusa, a king called Alaksandu and a people called the Ahhiyawa. Troy myth or reality, the real history behind the Trojan War, and the honest scholarly verdict on whether the Trojan War was real. With Christopher Nolan's film The Odyssey (2026) renewing worldwide interest in Homer's epics, this is the ancient history and archaeology behind the legend: Bronze Age warfare, the excavations at Troy from Schliemann onward, and what the Hittite records actually say.

  0:00 The horse in your computer

  3:23 The man who found Troy by destroying it

Transcript:

Your computer's security settings have a category called Trojan horse. That story is nearly three thousand years old, and the horse never appears in Homer's

Iliad. Not once. The version you actually picture was written centuries

later, by a Roman. But the hill is real. You can walk on it in north-west Turkey this afternoon. One layer down it is burnt black, with arrowheads in it and human bones nobody buried.

So. Does that mean the Trojan War really happened? Here is the strange part. That is not one question. Pull the story apart and you get about nine separate claims.

The horse. The thousand ships. The ten years. The gold. The heroes. They do not all get the same answer.

Some collapse the second you touch them. And one survives somewhere nobody was even looking, written down by clerks who had never heard of Homer, centuries

before he sang a note. That is the one I want to reach. I grew up being told this one was pure fiction. A poet's fantasy with gods in it. Finding out that it is not, or at least not all of it, quietly rearranged how I hear every other legend. So let us do this properly.

Piece by piece. Real, half real, or invented. And we keep score. So start with the piece we just broke.

The wooden horse. Enormous, hollow, left standing on the beach. Soldiers hidden inside. The Trojans drag it through their own gates and lose everything by morning. Everyone calls that the climax

of Homer's Iliad. But the Iliad covers a matter of weeks in the final year of the war, and it opens by asking a goddess to sing about one subject only. The rage of Achilles. That is the poem.

Not the war. And it ends with a funeral. Hector's funeral. No horse. No burning city. Not even the death of Achilles. So where does the horse come from? A few lines in the Odyssey.

The long cinematic version you actually picture is Virgil, a Roman writing in Latin roughly seven hundred years after Homer. The oldest surviving image

of it is scratched on a storage jar from around six hundred seventy BC. That is your evidence. A pot, and a Roman poet.

Nobody has ever dug up a giant wooden horse. Verdict.

Not Homer's. Not evidence. Bolted on afterwards. One down. And that was the easy one.

Next. The thousand ships. Was this the face that launched a thousand ships. Everybody knows the line.

Almost everybody thinks it is Homer. It is Christopher Marlowe, printed in London in sixteen oh four. That sentence is Elizabethan English. It is nearer in time to you than it is to Homer. Homer never gives a fleet total

at all. He gives a list, and adding up his own figures lands you around twelve hundred, a total generally read as poetry rather than a manifest. The ten-year siege? The poems say ten years.

The ground says nothing about ten years. And the famous date, eleven eighty-four

BC, is one scholar's back-calculation, made around two hundred twenty BC. The Greeks could not even agree among themselves, guessing across a century

and a half. One guess happened to stick. But hold on.

Because that ship list does something odd. The Greece it describes, which towns are big and which ones matter, fits the Bronze Age better than it fits Homer's own century. He is reciting a map that had been dead for four hundred years.

Something real is fossilised inside the poem. Score it half real. Now the man. Everyone knows who found Troy.

Heinrich Schliemann. That is not what happened. The man who worked out where Troy was is called Frank Calvert. He owned the eastern half of that hill and had been cutting trenches into it since eighteen sixty-three, seven years

before Schliemann turned up. Britannica says Calvert deserves the lion's share of the responsibility for siting Troy at Hisarlik.

Calvert had the right hill and no money. Schliemann had money.

And in his first archaeological book, Schliemann laid out Calvert's argument with Calvert's

name quietly removed. Schliemann was not an archaeologist. He was a businessman who retired at thirty-six to go looking for Homer.

If you saw our Odyssey episode, you know how that went.

He drove a trench straight down through the heart of the mound and smashed past the exact

layers that are today's leading candidates. Look at an excavation map of Troy now and there is a blank space near the centre with a label on it.

Palace removed by Schliemann. Then there is the gold he called the treasure of King

Priam. Real gold. Wrong city.

Roughly a thousand years too early for any Trojan War anyone can argue

for. Verdict on both. False, and false.

Which leaves the obvious question. What was actually down there?

Not a lost city in a jungle. A mound people kept knocking down and rebuilding on for more than three thousand years. Nine cities in one hill.

But here is the question almost nobody asks. Whose city was it?

In the story, the Trojans are basically Greeks with worse luck. They speak Greek. They pray to Greek gods. In reality, Troy

was not Greek. It was Anatolian. Its wall towers follow a Hittite plan. Its diplomatic world was the Hittite empire, inland to the

east. And the only piece of writing ever recovered from a prehistoric level at Troy is a tiny bronze seal, inscribed in Hittite hieroglyphs.

Not one word of Greek in the entire city. So why would anyone sail across a sea to fight over it?

Look at where it sits. At the mouth of the strait between the Aegean and the

Black Sea. Ancient ships often had to wait near Troy for a wind to carry them up the channel. Ships still queue in that strait today, for

the same geography. And in nineteen eighty-eight Manfred Korfmann found what everyone had missed. Troy was not just the citadel. A lower city stretched away to the south, making the site by his estimate ten to fifteen times bigger than the fortress everyone had been digging.

Not everyone believed him. Hold that thought. Verdict.

The war story is Greek. The city was not. Now the turn.

Everything so far has been the legend falling apart in your hands. This is where the ground pushes back. Because a city on that hill

really was destroyed. Twice. And the two destructions could

not be more different. Troy VI, the beautiful one with the walls, comes down around thirteen hundred BC. Walls tipped off true, heavy blocks thrown around. Most experts read that as an earthquake. The city was shaken down, not stormed. So they rebuilt.

Troy VIIa has the same walls and a completely different life inside them.

Big airy houses chopped into small rooms. Storage jars sunk into

the floors everywhere. New houses shoved flush against the inside of the defensive wall. Some gates blocked up. That is not a prosperous city. That is a city cramming people and food behind its walls, waiting for something.

And then, somewhere between about twelve twenty and eleven eighty BC, it burns. In places there is up to three feet of blackened debris. There are arrowheads.

There is military equipment. And there are human remains lying unburied, which matters, because the earlier destruction layers at Troy do not have them. Nobody came back for these ones. In twenty twenty-five the excavators

found a dense cache of sling stones packed into a small patch of ground outside the palace. Korfmann had made the argument years earlier.

Winners pick their sling bullets back up. A heap left where it fell suggests the people who threw them lost. So. A fortified city, on

exactly the hill the Greeks pointed at, at roughly the right time, sacked and burned with bodies left in the open. Verdict.

Real. Physically, undeniably real.

But the ground does not tell you who did it. There is nothing in the archaeological evidence to identify precisely who the attackers were. A fire with no name on it. So where does a name come from? Not from Greece. Greece had gone

dark. Between roughly twelve fifty and eleven fifty BC the whole eastern Mediterranean came apart. Mycenaean palaces burned. The Hittite empire fell. Writing systems vanished.

Greece produced no written records at all for something like four centuries. So whatever happened at Troy could travel only one way.

In songs, mouth to mouth in the dark, until the Greeks borrowed an alphabet from the Phoenicians. Scholars are not even certain Homer existed as one

person. The Greek evidence is a rumour of a rumour.

Which is why the best evidence for the Trojan War is not Greek at all. It is twenty-six clay tablets from the archives of the Hittite capital, Hattusa. Fifteenth to thirteenth centuries BC. Baked clay.

Bureaucracy. Treaties and letters, filed and forgotten. And they keep mentioning a people the Hittites called the Ahhiyawa.

Most scholars read Ahhiyawa as a Hittite spelling of Achaioi. The Achaeans. Which is exactly what Homer calls the Greeks.

The same tablets name a city out in the north-west. They call it Wilusa. And inside Homer's own verse there is a fossil. The rhythm of the lines

shows that Ilion, the Greek name for Troy, was once pronounced with a w on the front. Wilion. Wilusa. Wilion.

It is not proven. It is also not nothing. And then it gets stranger.

One Hittite treaty, from around twelve ninety-five to twelve seventy-two BC, records the great king Muwatalli making a formal agreement with the king of Wilusa.

And the king of Wilusa has a name. Alaksandu. Now.

Paris, the Trojan prince who takes Helen, wife of Menelaus of Sparta, and starts the whole war, carries a second name in the Iliad.

Alexandros. Be careful with that. Alaksandu is a king and Paris is only a prince, and nobody can explain why an Anatolian ruler carried a Greek-looking name. Scholars argue about it and have not settled it. But sit with the shape of the thing.

A Hittite scribe, centuries before Homer, writing out a dull treaty with a real king of a real city called Wilusa.

There is one more letter. In the middle of the thirteenth century BC, a Hittite great king, probably Hattusili the Third, writes to the king of the Ahhiyawa.

And in passing, he refers back to Wilusa as something the two of them had once gone to war over, and had since made peace about.

A war. Between the Hittites and, most likely, Mycenaean Greeks. Over, most likely, Troy. In an official letter.

The specialist J. D. Hawkins puts it plainly. Wilusa was a point of conflict between the Hittites and the Ahhiyawa.

Now be honest about the limits. That quarrel is between Hittites and Greeks, not Greeks and Trojans, and the text does not say whether it was a war, a raid, or a diplomatic row.

But nobody was making this fit. These tablets were written by clerks with no interest in Greek poetry, in a language no one could read for three thousand years, and they sat buried the entire time. Verdict.

The city is real. The names are real. A quarrel over it is on record. The war in the poem still is not. Now the case against, because you have earned it. Frank Kolb spent years

arguing the opposite. Troy VI, he wrote, was not a commercial city, and it is still a live argument, not a settled result.

And a fire is not a war. People went on living at Troy for something like two hundred and fifty years after that fire. If we had never inherited the Greek legend, nobody digging that black layer would have leapt straight to a foreign invasion.

So here is the honest scorecard. The horse, not Homer's.

The thousand ships, Elizabethan. The ten years and the famous date, literature. Schliemann finding Troy, no. Calvert did. Priam's treasure, wrong city by

a thousand years. Troy as a Greek town, no. A real fortified city on the right hill, yes. Burned violently at roughly the right time, yes. Named in foreign archives and quarrelled over by people the Hittites

called the Ahhiyawa, yes. Achilles, Hector, the gods, the duel, the horse. No evidence at all. Even Korfmann, the excavator

who most wanted Homer to be true, would only say it is more likely than not that there were armed conflicts around Troy, and that Homer's account rests on a memory of real events. More likely than not. That is the strongest honest claim

on the table. So in the end, believing or disbelieving in the Trojan War is an act of faith, whichever side you pick. That is what this one

did to me. It did not turn the legend into history. It taught me that made up and remembered badly are not the same thing, and that we are far too quick to file a story under fiction just because the version

that reached us has monsters in it. Which brings us back to the hill. It is still there. Under your feet the black layer is real. The arrowheads are real. The unburied bones are real. The horse is the only part that is not.

Which means the one piece of this story that reached your computer is the

only piece that was never there. People believed every word of it for most of three thousand years. Then we called it all a fairy tale. And we were only right about the good bits. Four hundred years of songs

in the dark, and the singers still knew which hill.

Subscribe and stay with me, because the next one is the hardest turn we have ever

taken. We are leaving the Aegean for West Africa, and the Mali Empire.

The richest human being in all of recorded history was a medieval West African

king. And the empire he inherited was founded, by

its own legend, by a prince who could not walk. That is next.

## Was Atlantis Ever Real? (Plato Invented It)

URL: https://doodlehistory.com/episodes/atlantis/
Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0TYyYxa2_r0
Published: 2026-09-06 · Length: 12 min

The lost city of Atlantis is the most famous vanished civilization in history — but was it ever real? Everything humanity “knows” about it traces back to just two texts, written by a single philosopher: Plato. This is the true story behind the myth — how Atlantis was invented, why it refuses to die, and the real drowned cities hiding inside the legend.

Atlantis explained: what Plato actually wrote in the dialogues Timaeus and Critias around 360 BC, why historians and archaeologists agree Atlantis was invented as a philosophical allegory rather than a real place, and how a genuinely real Greek city — Helike — was swallowed by the sea in a single night in 373 BC, during Plato’s own lifetime. We cover whether Atlantis was real, the Minoan civilization and the colossal Thera (Santorini) eruption around 1600 BC, the failed searches from the “Eye of the Sahara” to the Bahamas’ Bimini Road, and how a congressman, Ignatius Donnelly, built the modern Atlantis myth in 1882. Part ancient history, part archaeology, part philosophy: how a Greek thought experiment became the world's most hunted lost civilization, and what genuinely sunken ancient cities tell us.

Right now, without even trying, you can picture Atlantis. The golden rings. The shining city. The whole thing sliding under the waves. You have carried that picture your whole life. And never once asked where it came from. So let me ruin it for you.

Every piece of it comes from one man. He set the whole story down, stopped

Stay with me. The answer is stranger than the myth.

And here is what I actually think, before we begin. This made-up city refuses to die because it is carrying something real.

Plato meant to write a third dialogue to finish it. He never did.

So the most famous ending in history has no ending. The city sinks in a line that

Forget the crystals. Forget the aliens. Here is the real story.

Sail west. Out past the Pillars of Heracles. What we call the Strait of Gibraltar. Out there, Plato says, sat an

The lands he knew as North Africa and Asia Minor. And a god built it. Poseidon, lord of the sea. He shaped the city in perfect rings. Circles of water and land, wrapped around a hill at the center.

That ringed city is the Atlantis on every map and every movie poster. A god drew it. In a story. On that island grew a mighty

When did all this happen? Here is where it gets absurd. Plato's story sets it nine thousand years before his own lifetime.

That is roughly eleven thousand six hundred years ago.

Older than any real city that has ever existed. Older than history itself. And how did Plato learn this ancient secret? Thirdhand.

An Egyptian priest told it to a Greek traveler named Solon.

Solon passed it to his family. It trickled down the generations. Then, at last, to Plato. A world-spanning empire. An eleven-thousand-year-old war. And the only paper trail is one long game of ancient telephone. Starting to smell it yet? So if it never existed, what was Plato doing?

Why invent an entire drowned world? Here is the twist. Plato was not writing history. He was writing a warning.

Atlantis is a foil. A villain built on purpose. Picture two kingdoms side by side. One is proud, rich, greedy,

And here is the uncomfortable part Plato was really pointing at. That arrogant, overreaching sea empire looked an awful lot like Athens itself. Plato had watched his own city build a navy, seize an empire, and lose a catastrophic war. Atlantis was a mirror. Held up to his own people.

This is what your pride will cost you. And think about who is telling

you this. Plato is the man who wrote the Allegory of the Cave.

Prisoners chained in the dark, watching shadows, certain they were seeing the whole

world. He built stories to teach. Atlantis is just another one. And you do not have to take my word for it. His own student saw straight through it. Aristotle, Plato's most famous pupil, reportedly called Atlantis an invention. The quip handed down through later writers goes like this.

The man who dreamed Atlantis up is the same man who sank it.

The very first Atlantis skeptic sat in Plato's own classroom.

So. Atlantis is a made-up morality tale. Case closed. Right? Here is the part nobody tells you.

Plato may have invented Atlantis. But he did not invent the sea swallowing a city. Because that happened. Right in front of him. This is where a lie starts hiding a truth. The year is

three hundred and seventy-three BC. On the Gulf of Corinth sits a real, thriving Greek city. Its name is Helike. And Helike is famous for one thing above all. A great sanctuary to Poseidon.

God of the sea. God of the earthquake. The very same god who, in Plato's tale, builds Atlantis. One winter night, the ground convulses. An earthquake rips the city open. Then the sea rears up behind it. By morning, Helike is gone.

Temples, people, Poseidon's own shrine, all dragged beneath the waves.

In a single night. Now count the years. Helike drowned around three hundred and seventy-three BC. Plato wrote Atlantis maybe ten years later. He was alive for it. He was in his prime. A real Greek city, sacred to the sea god, had

just vanished under the water overnight. The whole Greek world was talking about

it. And then he sat down and wrote about a city sacred to the sea god, that vanished under the water overnight. Many scholars think that is no accident. That Helike is the real ghost haunting the legend. But be careful. Helike is not Atlantis.

Helike was a town on a gulf, not a continent out in the Atlantic.

It may only have handed Plato his most unforgettable image.

And Helike is not the only ghost. Go back much further.

Around sixteen hundred BC, on the island we now call Santorini, a volcano

named Thera exploded. It was one of the largest eruptions in

all of human history. It blew the entire middle out of the island.

It carved the curved cliffs you can still stand on today.

The blast flung ash and giant waves across the sea, straight at Crete. And on Crete lived the Minoans. Europe's first great sea power. Wealthy, advanced, in love with the ocean. The eruption did not wipe them out in a night. But many scholars believe it crippled them.

The beginning of a long, slow fall for a brilliant maritime world. Sound familiar? A proud, advanced sea civilization, broken by nature.

Again, be honest. Thera sat in the Aegean, not beyond Gibraltar.

It happened over a thousand years before Plato, nothing like his invented date.

It is not Atlantis either. But look at what these ghosts share.

A shining sea power, thriving one moment.

Swallowed by the earth the next. That fear was real.

That memory was real. Plato did not invent the terror of the sea rising

to erase you. He inherited it. But maybe you are still hoping.

Maybe there is a real sunken continent out there, waiting to be found.

For over a century, people have looked. Seriously looked.

And here is their problem. We have now mapped the floor of the Atlantic Ocean.

An island the size of a country would leave a scar you could see from orbit.

A drowned shelf. A sunken mountain range.

There is nothing there. And the rock itself refuses to play along.

Continents are made of light, buoyant crust. It floats.

It cannot simply sink into the deep ocean and disappear.

The geology forbids it. None of that has stopped anyone.

The list of places crowned the real Atlantis is long, and gloriously desperate.

Santorini. The Azores. The Mid-Atlantic Ridge.

Antarctica. A line of rocks in the Bahamas called the Bimini Road, which turned out to be perfectly ordinary stone. Then there is the Eye of

the Sahara. A giant bullseye of rock in the African desert, famous

all over the internet. One small problem.

It sits over a thousand feet above the sea, hundreds of miles inland.

It has never once been underwater. My personal favorite is Spain.

A few years back, someone spotted mysterious circular shapes in a Spanish nature park. Atlantis, at last. They were fish ponds. Experimental tanks, dug in two thousand four, to raise zooplankton. One archaeologist counted around a dozen serious candidates for the lost city.

Every single one falls apart. Because you cannot find a place that was never a place.

Which leaves one final mystery. If Plato's Atlantis had no crystals, no

super technology, no lost master race, where did all of that come from?

Not from the ancient world. From a bookshop. In

eighteen eighty-two, an American congressman named Ignatius Donnelly published a book. And he took Plato completely literally. He argued that Atlantis was real, impossibly advanced, and the secret mother of every civilization on Earth.

Egypt, the Americas, all of it, children of Atlantis.

None of it was true. It did not matter. The book was a runaway bestseller, reprinted edition after edition. Almost everything you picture when

you hear the word Atlantis comes from Donnelly.

Not from Plato. Then it got stranger.

A few years later, the occultist Helena Blavatsky folded Atlantis into her mystical religion. Now the Atlanteans became a lost root race of humanity.

Psychic. Superhuman. A vanished mankind before mankind.

The crystals, the psychic god-beings, eventually the aliens.

That entire modern Atlantis was bolted on in the last hundred and fifty years. Long after Plato was dust. And it never stopped. It is in your superhero

movies. Your video games. Your streaming documentaries, still hunting a lost super

civilization tonight. You have been handed a Victorian fantasy wearing an ancient Greek mask. So. Was Atlantis ever real?

Here is the honest verdict. As Plato described it, a super civilization in the Atlantic that sank eleven thousand years ago, no.

It never existed. No continent. No ruins.

No trace. He invented it. But do not walk away thinking it was only a lie. Because the legend is true. Just not in the way you wanted it to be.

It is true the way a scar is true. Plato's Atlantis is a memory of real

terror. The sea really does swallow cities.

Ask Helike. Great sea powers really do fall to disaster.

Ask the Minoans. Atlantis was never lost, because it was never a place. It was a fear. Maybe the oldest one we carry. That everything you build can be erased in a single night.

That is why I cannot call Atlantis a lie. It is the truest thing we ever invented about the sea. And maybe that is why it will not die.

In an age of rising seas and drowning coastlines, a great civilization swallowed by the ocean no longer sounds like a fairy tale.

It sounds like a forecast. Now sit with one last thought.

If a single city vanishing in a night could echo for two thousand years, imagine

The eruption of Thera. The day the Bronze Age world nearly

ended. But that is a story for another day. Subscribe, and follow

And some of those cities were real.

## Was the Samurai Honour Code Even Real?

URL: https://doodlehistory.com/episodes/sengoku-japan/
Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=t_qFKPlWgqU
Published: 2026-09-03 · Length: 12 min

The calm, honour-bound samurai you picture, loyal unto death and living by an ancient code called bushido, is largely a myth. This is the real history of Sengoku Japan: roughly a century and a half of civil war, peasant gun-armies and constant betrayal, and how the famous samurai honour code was actually written down long after the fighting had already stopped.

Sengoku Japan explained, from the Onin War of 1467 to the Tokugawa peace. We follow how Portuguese matchlock guns and conscripted ashigaru foot soldiers changed samurai warfare, the three unifiers who put Japan back together (Oda Nobunaga, Toyotomi Hideyoshi and Tokugawa Ieyasu), the Honno-ji betrayal of 1582, and the Battle of Sekigahara in 1600, where one lord's mid-battle defection ended the Warring States period in a single afternoon. Then how bushido as a fixed honour code was systematised in the peaceful Edo period and carried around the world by Nitobe Inazo's book around 1900. Was the samurai honour code even real? Here is what the history actually shows. A military history of feudal Japan: civil war, castle sieges, samurai armies, and the battles of Nagashino and Sekigahara that ended an age of war and bought 250 years of peace.

Chapters:
  0:00 The Samurai You Picture
  1:44 Kyoto Burns: The Onin War
  3:06 Peasants, Spears and Portuguese Guns
  4:39 The Three Unifiers and a Culture of Betrayal
  6:51 One Afternoon, One Traitor: Sekigahara
  8:09 The Long Peace and the Closed Country
  8:44 The Code Written After the War

  - Medievalists.net — Karl Friday on the samurai / bushido myth (https://www.medievalists.net/2022/04/bushido-and-what-bushi-did-loyalty-reputation-and-honor-in-the-samurai-tradition/)

Transcript:

The honour-bound samurai in your head is loyal to a code that had not been written down yet. That calm, spotless warrior from the show Shogun and a hundred video games? He supposedly lived and died by an ancient way of

the warrior called bushido. But that code was mostly tidied into its neat, famous form generations after the real fighting had already stopped.

And the version that conquered the world was written in English, for foreigners, around the year nineteen hundred. Here is the other half of the shock.

The war that built the whole samurai legend lasted roughly a century and a half. Then it ended in a single afternoon, because one lord turned his army

on his own side. And here is the idea I cannot shake. We only ever turn a brutal war into a beautiful legend once

we are safely on the far side of it. So the code came after the killing. And the killing came with almost no fixed code at all.

That is the story nobody prints on the poster. Once you see it, you can never watch a samurai the same way again.

You already know the image in your head. A lone samurai in perfect armour, sword raised, calm as still water.

Loyal to his lord unto death. Honest. Fearless. Bound by an ancient code of honour called bushido. When he fails, he kneels and takes his own life rather than live in shame. It is beautiful, and it is absolutely

everywhere. It runs through samurai films, through the show Shogun, through a hundred video games. Some of it even leaked into the Jedi of Star Wars.

There is just one problem with this flawless warrior. The men who actually fought Japan's great wars would barely recognise him.

To meet the real samurai, you have to walk into a burning city.

The year is fourteen sixty-seven. Japan has a shogun, a supreme military ruler, named Ashikaga Yoshimasa. But Yoshimasa is weak, and he cannot decide who should inherit his seat.

That single family argument lights a fuse. Two great warrior clans take sides and drag their armies into the capital, Kyoto. This is the Onin War, and it does not stop for ten years.

Kyoto, the jewel of Japan, is looted, and then it is set on fire. Temples burn. Shops are ransacked. Hostages are massacred. One modern history calls it simply an orgy of violence.

When the smoke finally clears, the capital is a ruin, and the shogun rules almost nothing. Real power drains out into the countryside, into the hands of

local warlords called daimyo. Each daimyo carves out his own little kingdom, with his own castle and his own private army. For the next century and a half, they fight each other almost without pause.

The Japanese have a chilling name for the spirit of this age. Gekokujo. The low overthrow the high.

Servants murder their masters. Vassals topple their lords. Peasants seize castles. Loyalty here is not sacred. Loyalty is a deal, and deals get broken.

So if betrayal was routine, who was actually doing the fighting?

Here is where the legend really starts to crack. Forget the elegant duel between two noble swordsmen. The daimyo needed bodies, thousands

of them, and they needed them fast. So they shoved long spears into the hands of ordinary farmers. These conscripted commoners were called

ashigaru, the light-footed foot soldiers. Peasants in cheap armour, not born warriors, now made up the bulk of every army.

And then, in fifteen forty-three, something washed up on a beach that changed everything. A storm drove a Portuguese ship onto the little island of Tanegashima.

On board were traders carrying matchlock muskets. The local lord bought a couple of guns, and Japanese smiths copied them within months. Soon workshops all over the country were mass-producing firearms.

You cannot teach a peasant the sword in a year. But you can teach him to point a gun and pull a trigger in a week. One young warlord understood exactly what that

meant. His name was Oda Nobunaga. Nobunaga built whole units of matchlock gunners, hundreds of them at first, later thousands.

And in fifteen seventy-five, at a place called Nagashino, he proved his point in blood. Facing him was the Takeda clan, whose cavalry was the most feared in

all Japan. Nobunaga lined his gunners up behind a long wall of wooden stakes. As the famous horsemen thundered forward, massed volleys

of gunfire tore into them. Wave after wave of Japan's proudest riders went down before they could land a single blow. By some accounts the Takeda

lost thousands of men in that one afternoon. The age of the mounted samurai hero was ending, and gunpowder was the thing ending it.

Out of all this chaos, three men would drag Japan back into one piece. There is an old saying about them, passed down for centuries.

Nobunaga mixed the rice cake. Hideyoshi shaped it. Ieyasu ate it. Three warlords, one country, and a mountain of betrayal

stacked between them. Oda Nobunaga was the first, and the most ruthless. He marched into Kyoto, installed a puppet shogun, and

made himself the strongest man in Japan. By fifteen eighty-two he controlled roughly half the entire country. Nothing on the battlefield could stop him.

So in the end, he was not stopped on a battlefield at all. Here is the part nobody tells you about the man who almost united Japan. He was destroyed by one of his own generals, a man named Akechi Mitsuhide.

One night in Kyoto, Akechi turned his army around and surrounded Nobunaga inside a temple called Honno-ji. Trapped, with the building burning around him, Nobunaga took his own life. The greatest warlord of the age, betrayed by his own

trusted officer. And Akechi's reward for the perfect betrayal? He held power for barely two weeks. Because another of Nobunaga's generals

came racing back to avenge him. His name was Toyotomi Hideyoshi, and his story is the strangest of them all. Hideyoshi was not born a lord.

He was born a peasant. By tradition, he started his career carrying another man's sandals. And this peasant clawed and schemed his way up until he ruled the whole

of Japan. In a world supposedly built on noble bloodlines, a farmer's son ended up on top. But Hideyoshi remembered exactly

where he came from, and the memory frightened him. So in fifteen eighty-eight he ordered a great sword hunt across the land. His men went village to village,

stripping the weapons from every peasant they found. From that day on, only samurai were allowed to carry a blade. Farmers would farm.

Warriors would fight. And nobody could ever climb the way he had. He froze Japanese society solid, just as the fighting was finally winding

down. Then, in fifteen ninety-eight, Hideyoshi died. And he handed his brand new empire to a five-year-old boy.

You can already feel what is coming next. A small child on the throne, and a country crawling with hungry warlords. The whole thing was about to be decided, once

and for all, in a single day. The date is the twenty-first of October, sixteen hundred. Two enormous coalitions line up against each other in a misty valley

called Sekigahara. On one side stands Tokugawa Ieyasu, the last of the three unifiers. On the other stands Ishida Mitsunari, fighting

to protect the dead ruler's little son. By many accounts, something like eighty thousand men stood on each side. This is the battle

that will decide who owns Japan. The fighting opens in the morning fog, and for hours it hangs perfectly in the balance. And then every

eye turns to look at one quiet hill. On that hill sits a young lord named Kobayakawa Hideaki, with a huge, fresh, untouched

army. He is supposed to be fighting for Ishida's side. But in secret, he has already struck a deal with the enemy. Around midday, Kobayakawa finally makes his choice.

He charges his whole army down the hill, straight into his own allies. It is the single most important betrayal in Japanese history. His allies, stabbed in the back, simply crumble and break.

Seeing it, other lords switch sides too, one after another. By early afternoon, it is finished. A war that had burned for roughly a century and a half ended in one afternoon. Because one man on a hill could not be trusted.

Tokugawa Ieyasu was now the master of all Japan. In sixteen oh three, the emperor named him shogun.

He ruled from a small town called Edo. You know that town today by its newer name. Tokyo. And then the man who won by

war did something remarkable. He killed war itself. Ieyasu and his heirs tore down castles and bound the warlords with strict rules.

Then they shut the entire country's doors against the outside world. Christianity was banned. Foreigners were expelled. Even leaving Japan became a

crime. For more than two hundred and fifty years, the great wars simply stopped. And this is where the greatest twist of the whole story begins.

Think about what a samurai actually is now. There are no more battles left to fight. An entire warrior class, sitting in a peaceful country, with nothing

to do. They became clerks. Administrators. Men who shuffled paper and collected a salary. A killer with no one left

to kill has to become something else. So the samurai quietly reinvented themselves, on paper. In the long peace, scholars sat down to answer

one very hard question. If a warrior never goes to war, what on earth is he actually for? One of them was a thoughtful man named Yamaga Soko, writing in the late sixteen hundreds.

He and others began polishing the scattered old warrior values into a single neat system. Service. Discipline.

Honour. Loyalty unto death. The exact code we now imagine the Sengoku samurai all lived by. It was largely written down after those Sengoku samurai

were already gone. Now be careful here, because the real truth is subtle. Samurai did have values during the wars. Courage, skill, reputation, all of that was genuinely real.

But there was never one fixed, written code that every samurai everywhere obeyed. Those values shifted from century to century, and from one lord to the next. One historian puts it bluntly.

Much of what people think they know about the samurai, he says, is a mythology that barely resembles the real history. And money, records admit, was often

the real reason a samurai marched to war at all. Then one small book

carried the polished dream around the entire world. Around the year nineteen hundred, a Japanese writer named Nitobe Inazo published it. He wrote it in English, for Western readers,

and titled it Bushido, the Soul of Japan. By then, the samurai class itself had already been abolished for decades.

Nitobe handed the West a clean, gentle, romantic warrior with seven perfect virtues. The world fell in love with that warrior instantly.

And that romantic warrior is the one living in your head right this second. He is why samurai films still feel like sacred scripture.

He is why leadership books quote bushido today as ancient, timeless wisdom. A code barely a century old, sold to you as if it were a thousand years old.

None of this makes the real samurai small. They existed. They were brave. They fought and bled for a century and a half.

But the spotless, unbreakable code of honour was polished up long after the blood had dried. The war itself was messy, greedy, and decided by a traitor on a hill. The beautiful code was tidied in peacetime, and finished

off in an English book. So the next time you picture that flawless, honour-bound samurai, remember one thing. The men who actually did the fighting would have found him strange.

Their world ran on gunfire, hired peasants, and broken promises, not on a spotless code. The code came after the war. And that, almost always,

is exactly when a legend gets written. So maybe that is the real lesson buried under all this blood. Peace does not just end a war. It quietly rewrites it into a legend we would rather remember.

That is the part that stays with me. We remember the beautiful version, because someone sat down, safe in peacetime, and carefully wrote it for us.

Next time on Doodle History, we chase a legend with no war behind it at all. A drowned empire that may never have existed in the first place. Atlantis. Subscribe, and come find out how much of that story was ever real.

## Why Did Pompeii's Victims Die in One Second? (Vesuvius 79 AD)

URL: https://doodlehistory.com/episodes/pompeii/
Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=eJFqlM6W1xc
Published: 2026-08-30 · Length: 11 min

In 79 AD, Mount Vesuvius buried the Roman city of Pompeii in a single day. But almost everything we were taught about how its people died is wrong. This is the true story of Pompeii and the eruption of Vesuvius: an ordinary Roman town, the warnings it ignored, and the forensic science of what really happened in its final hours.

A full history of Pompeii and the 79 AD eruption of Mount Vesuvius, explained. How did the people of Pompeii really die? Why are the famous plaster casts not actually bodies? How did most of the city escape, and who was left behind? We follow the only eyewitness account, written by Pliny the Younger, the death of his uncle Pliny the Elder, the buried town of Herculaneum, the pyroclastic surges, and why the eruption date, traditionally the 24th of August, may really have been in October. Plus why three million people still live in the shadow of Vesuvius today. This is ancient history and archaeology at their most human: a Roman city, a volcanic eruption, and the modern excavation science of plaster casts, scans and digs that finally explained what happened.

Transcript:

Almost everything you were taught about how the people of Pompeii died is wrong. They did not slowly suffocate under the falling ash. Most of them were dead in

under one second. A wall of gas so hot it killed them before they could take a

single breath. And their own bones still prove it.

It looks staged. It looks impossible. And every single piece of it actually

happened. But the part that stays with me is how ordinary it all was. These were not monsters from history. They were just people in the middle of a normal day that turned out to be their last.

This is Pompeii. Let me show you how a whole city got frozen mid-life.

Because to understand what really happened here, you have to rewind to the day before anyone

was afraid. Pompeii was not a ruin. It was a boom town.

A busy Roman port on the Bay of Naples, packed with maybe eleven

to fifteen thousand people. About one in three of them were enslaved.

This was a city that loved money, wine, and a good scandal. It was rich, loud, and completely alive. For everyone here, that

morning was just another day of business as usual.

And when the ash finally sealed the city, it sealed that single ordinary day,

perfectly. In a bakery, loaves of bread were found still inside the oven, some stamped with the baker's own mark.

On the walls, thousands of painted notices survive, endorsing candidates in the

next election. There is casual graffiti too, including a gladiator praised as the sighed for joy of the girls. One mosaic on a floor simply

reads, profit is joy. There is even a brothel, its walls

still covered in painted scenes. You can still walk these streets today, past the shops, the fountains and the bakeries. It is the most complete snapshot

of daily Roman life that exists anywhere on Earth. So how did a thriving, everyday

city turn into a graveyard of plaster ghosts? Because there is something the postcards never show you. This shiny town was already broken.

Seventeen years earlier, on the fifth of February, a massive earthquake had torn through the region. Statues split.

Flocks of sheep dropped dead. The philosopher Seneca wrote it all down.

It was the biggest warning the city would ever get. And seventeen years later, Pompeii

was still fixing the damage. The forum stood under scaffolding. Houses sat half repaired. Then, in the final days, the ground began

to shake again. And nobody panicked. Small quakes were normal here. Just the earth grumbling, the way it always did.

And here is the tragedy nobody tells you. They did not run, because they did not

know what the mountain was. To them, Vesuvius was just a quiet green mountain on the horizon. Almost nobody clearly understood it was a volcano

at all. So when it finally spoke, they had no idea what they were hearing.

Around the middle of the day, the mountain answered. A towering column of ash and pumice punched straight up into the sky. It rose roughly thirty

kilometres high, higher than any storm cloud. At its peak, it may have reached thirty three. From the streets of Pompeii, it must

have looked like the sky itself was tearing open. A teenager named Pliny the Younger was watching it from across the bay. He was just seventeen years old, safe at

a naval base called Misenum. He saw the cloud rise on a single trunk, then

split off into branches, like an umbrella pine. Years later, the historian

Tacitus asked him to describe what he had seen. So he wrote it down from memory, in two letters that still survive. It is the only eyewitness account of

the disaster that we have. And the most violent kind of eruption is still called Plinian today, named after that one boy's letter.

And here is the part that still divides experts, right now.

We might have the date of the most famous eruption in history completely wrong.

For centuries the textbooks said it was the twenty fourth of August.

But that date comes from a copy of a copy of Pliny's letter.

The original is lost. Then, in twenty eighteen, diggers found a charcoal scrawl on a wall. Add to that autumn fruit in the ruins, walnuts, figs and pomegranates, and victims found wearing warm clothes.

So many researchers now argue it actually happened in autumn, around October. The Pompeii park still officially defends August, and the argument is not settled.

Two thousand years on, we cannot even agree what day the sky fell. It is a genuine mystery, still hiding in the ruins. But whatever the date, the

beginning was slow. For about eighteen hours, pumice and ash rained down on the town. It piled up more than two metres deep, until roofs

cracked and collapsed under the weight. The falling ash blotted out the sun, and midday turned into a choking black night. And here is the fact that

changes the whole story. That slow first phase was an escape window.

And most of Pompeii used it. Thousands of people grabbed what they could carry and fled toward the sea. Whole families simply walked out and never

came back. So far, only about one thousand one hundred and fifty bodies have ever been found in Pompeii. And that is the number recovered, not the number

who died. Even today, only about two thirds of the town has been dug up at all. So the casts you saw at the start are not the whole city.

They are the ones who waited too long. The ones who thought the worst was already over. It was not. For those who stayed behind, there was

nowhere left to run. While thousands fled, one man sailed straight toward the mountain. Pliny the Elder, the boy's own uncle, commanded

the Roman fleet across the bay at Misenum. He launched his warships toward the eruption, partly to study it, and partly to rescue people from the shore.

And his young nephew stood on the far coast, watching him sail away. It was the last time the boy would ever see him alive. His uncle, they say, was

entirely fearless, calling out each new phase to be written down exactly as he saw it. He landed south of the volcano, at a town called Stabiae, and sheltered

with his friend Pomponianus for the night. He is the only Roman admiral known to have died leading a rescue. But that death was still hours

away. First, the mountain had to change its weapon. Around one in the morning, the giant column could no longer hold itself up. It collapsed. And that is when Pompeii's real killer was born.

Not lava. There was never any flowing lava here at all.

Instead, avalanches of superheated gas and ash came racing down the slopes. Scientists call them pyroclastic surges.

The nearby town of Herculaneum was closer to the mountain, so it went first. It was buried under more than twenty metres of scorching debris.

In the nineteen eightys, archaeologists made a heartbreaking discovery on Herculaneum's old shoreline. Around three hundred people had crammed into stone

boathouses on the beach. They were waiting for rescue ships that would never come. That is exactly where the surge caught them. Then, the next morning, around

half past six, the surges reached Pompeii. And this is where I can finally

prove what I told you at the very start. The people here did not slowly choke to death on the ash. A forensic study, led by the volcanologist

Giuseppe Mastrolorenzo, measured what really happened. Even ten kilometres from the vent, the surge was still two hundred fifty to three hundred

degrees. That is hot enough to kill instantly, even for people hiding indoors. Most victims died of thermal shock in a fraction of a second,

before they could breathe in enough ash to suffocate. And we can prove it. Their bones are pale yellow, exactly the colour of bone heated to that temperature.

And most bodies are frozen in life like, mid action poses, muscles locked at the instant of death. It is a phenomenon called cadaveric spasm,

the body seizing up at the very moment of death. That is why the casts look like they are still moving. That is death arriving faster than fear.

At Herculaneum, closer to the vent, the heat was even worse, perhaps around five hundred degrees. It was so intense it vaporised soft

tissue almost instantly. Some skulls there even show signs of boiling from the inside. One recent study reported that a victim's brain had been turned to glass by the heat. And that same morning, at

Stabiae, the fearless old admiral finally fell. His ships lay trapped by the wind and the falling debris, unable to escape. Pliny the Elder died on the shore, exactly where he had gone to help.

Then the strangest thing of all happened. The world forgot. For more than sixteen hundred years, Pompeii lay silent under the fields.

By then, the whole town lay sealed under several metres of ash and pumice.

A buried city, remembered by almost no one, slowly fading

into a rumour. Digging first began nearby at Herculaneum, in the year seventeen thirty-eight. Then in seventeen forty-eight, workers

for King Charles of Bourbon broke through into Pompeii itself. And they found a whole town, frozen in a single day.

The bread in the ovens. The graffiti on the walls. The paintings still bright. But the people themselves were missing.

The bodies had rotted away long ago. All they left behind were strange hollow pockets in the hardened ash. For over a century, diggers broke straight through those pockets,

never realising what they were. Then in eighteen sixty-three, the director of the excavations, Giuseppe Fiorelli, finally understood. They were people shaped holes. Perfect molds of the dead. So he poured liquid plaster inside, and he

waited. And Pompeii's victims came back. One by one, empty spaces in the ash became men, women and children again.

Faces. Folds of clothing. The exact pose of the final second.

The same trick even revealed doors, furniture, and a dog still chained in a courtyard.

Each cast is a person, caught in the very last thing they ever did.

And that is what you saw at the very beginning. Not a body. A cast of the empty space a body left behind. The person is gone. Only the shape of their last moment remains.

And the mountain? It is still there. Vesuvius erupted again as recently as nineteen forty-four, and it is still very much active. Today

around six hundred thousand people live in its official red zone, on its slopes. Roughly three million more live in greater Naples, in its shadow.

No active volcano on Earth has this many people standing this close to it.

Italy keeps the most ambitious evacuation plan in the world, ready to clear the red zone in seventy two hours. But the plan assumes about two weeks of warning.

Vesuvius may not give it. Pompeii is now one of the most visited places on Earth, and the casts are why. Pompeii is not really a story about the past.

It is a warning that never expired. The countdown that started two thousand years ago never

actually stopped. It only paused. And standing over those casts, that is what hits you hardest. They are not monsters from history. They are us, caught mid-sentence.

If you want to be here when it reaches zero, subscribe. There is a new story every Thursday. Next time on Countdown to Catastrophe,

we leave the ash behind for a world of samurai, shoguns and endless civil war. Feudal Japan.

---

## Why Did Alexander the Great's Empire Die With Him?

URL: https://doodlehistory.com/episodes/alexander/
Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=IcWKYqOmP0U
Published: 2026-08-27 · Length: 11 min

Alexander the Great built the largest empire the ancient world had yet seen — and it shattered within two years of his death. This is the history of the Macedonian Empire: its lightning rise under Alexander and its sudden, brutal collapse.

How did Alexander the Great's empire fall apart so fast? From Philip the Second's Macedonian war machine and the eighteen-foot sarissa phalanx, through the battles of Granicus, Issus and the decisive clash at Gaugamela against Darius the Third of Persia, to the siege of Tyre, the mutiny at the Hyphasis in India, and the deathbed answer "to the strongest" — this is the full story of Alexander the Great explained: the conquest of the Persian Empire, his death at thirty-two in Babylon, and the Wars of the Diadochi that tore his empire apart into the Hellenistic successor kingdoms of Ptolemaic Egypt, the Seleucid Empire and Antigonid Macedon. A military history of the ancient world: Alexander's campaigns from Macedonia to India, the sieges that built an empire in thirteen years, and the successor wars that tore it apart.
