Transcript:

The most powerful man on earth is dying, and he is only thirty-two years old. His generals crowd the bed with one question. Who gets it all? As the story goes, he answers in three words. To the strongest. Then he is gone, his generals look at each other, and they take him literally.

Here is what I keep coming back to. Conquering the world and keeping it are two completely different skills, and Alexander only ever mastered the first one.

Here is the strange part. This was the largest empire the world had yet seen, built in about thirteen years by a man who, by some accounts, never lost a single battle. And it took his own men less than two years to start

ripping it apart. So how does the biggest thing anyone had ever built vanish almost the moment its maker dies?

That is the question this whole story is counting down to.

And it ends in that room in Babylon. But to understand how it fell, you

have to see how it was built. And here is the first thing nobody tells you. Alexander did not build his war machine. His father did.

Rewind to three hundred fifty-nine BC. A man named Philip becomes king of Macedon. Macedon is a rough, half-wild kingdom on

the edge of the Greek world, sneered at by the polished cities to the south.

Philip changes everything. He takes an army of maybe ten thousand foot soldiers and builds it into twenty-four thousand. He grows the cavalry from a few hundred horsemen into thousands. He turns farmers into professionals.

Paid. Drilled. Uniformed. Sworn by oath to the king. Then he hands them a new weapon.

The sarissa. A pike roughly eighteen feet long. Twice the reach of a normal Greek spear. Picture a wall of men.

And out of that wall, several rows of iron points bristle forward all at once. You cannot get near them. And while those pikes pin you in place, Philip's

elite horsemen, the Companion Cavalry, come crashing into your flank. Hammer, and anvil. That was the machine. In three hundred thirty-eight BC,

Philip tests it at Chaeronea. Athens and Thebes throw their best at him, including the legendary Sacred Band of Thebes. Philip destroys them.

And a teenage boy leads a charge that day. He is eighteen. His name is Alexander. Philip is now master of Greece.

And he is planning something enormous. To invade Persia, the superpower of the

age. But he never gets to go. In three hundred thirty-six BC, at a wedding, Philip's own bodyguard steps forward and stabs him dead.

So the throne, the army, the whole grand plan, all of it lands on a twenty-year-old.

Half of Greece assumes the boy will crumble. They are wrong.

This boy was tutored as a teenager by Aristotle himself, one of the

sharpest minds who ever lived. And when Greece tests him, he moves so fast and so hard that the whole country falls back into line.

Then he does the unthinkable. He takes his father's plan, and his father's

army, and he crosses into Asia. He is going after the largest empire on earth with maybe forty to fifty thousand men.

And here is the part nobody tells you. That army is tiny next to what Persia

can throw at him. He is betting everything on winning fast. There is no plan B. There is no going home. three hundred thirty-four BC.

He crosses into Asia and wins his first great victory at a river called the Granicus.

Asia Minor swings open. three hundred thirty-three BC.

He meets the Persian king himself. Darius the Third, at the head of a far larger army, at a narrow coastal place called Issus.

Alexander charges straight at him. And the King of Kings panics. He turns his chariot and runs, leaving his own mother, his wife, and his

children behind on the field. Then comes the wall.

Tyre. An island fortress out in the sea, and it will not surrender. So Alexander does something insane.

He builds a road across the ocean. His army hauls rubble half a mile out into the water to reach the walls. Seven months later, Tyre falls.

Egypt does not even fight. It opens its gates.

And on the Nile, Alexander founds a city and stamps his own name on it. Alexandria. Remember that name. It outlives everything.

three hundred thirty-one BC. The rematch. Gaugamela. Darius has raised another vast army, far bigger than Alexander's

forty thousand. It does not matter. Alexander punches a gap in the Persian line, drives straight for the king, and Darius flees a second time.

The Persian Empire, two hundred years old, is finished.

The treasure cities fall like dominoes. Babylon. Susa. Persepolis. And in the ceremonial heart of Persia,

Alexander burns the great palace to the ground. Darius does not even die

a king. His own men murder him on the run.

Now there is no rival left anywhere. Alexander is hailed King of Asia.

But he does not stop. He pushes east, into years of brutal, grinding war in the mountains of Central Asia. Somewhere in there he

marries a noblewoman named Roxana. Remember her too.

And then, in three hundred twenty-six BC, in India, at a river called the Hydaspes, he meets a king named Porus.

And something Alexander has never faced before. War elephants. Dozens of them. A wall of grey giants. It is the bloodiest fight of his entire life. And he wins it. Even the elephants are not enough.

But this victory costs him something. Here is the part nobody tells

you about the man who conquered the world. His warhorse, Bucephalus, the stallion he tamed as a boy, the horse that carried him across an empire, dies

here in India. And Alexander, master of Persia, builds an entire city just to mark the grave of a horse. Alexander wants to keep going.

East, always east, chasing the edge of the world.

His men do not. And here, at a muddy river in India, the man who beat Persia finally meets the one enemy he cannot defeat.

His own army. Imagine you have followed one man for eight years. You have marched through seventy straight days of monsoon rain.

Your gear is rotting off your body. And now you hear that ahead of you wait even larger armies, and even more elephants.

So you stop. You simply refuse to take one more step east. That is what happens. The whole army sits down and says no.

Alexander rages. He shuts himself in his tent for days, waiting for them to change their minds. They do not. And for the first time in his life, Alexander the Great has

to turn around and go home. But the way home nearly finishes what

the enemy could not. He marches a huge part of his army through the Gedrosian Desert. Blistering heat. No water. No food.

And here is the cruel part. By some accounts, more of his soldiers died crossing that one desert than in all his famous battles combined. Not to Persians.

Not to elephants. To sand and thirst. He makes it back to Babylon.

He is only thirty-two years old. And this is the moment the whole story

has been counting down to. In June of three hundred twenty-three BC, after a banquet, Alexander falls ill. A fever takes hold.

For ten, maybe eleven days, it burns through him. And here is something we still argue about today. We do not actually know how he died.

Some say it was natural. Typhoid, or malaria, from the swamps

around Babylon. Others whisper it was poison, slipped to him by men in his own circle. The evidence has never settled it.

But the real disaster is not the fever. It is what is missing. Alexander is dying, and there is no one to inherit.

Think about that. He conquered the world, and he never secured the one thing that

actually mattered. His son is not even born yet. Roxana is still pregnant. His only other male relative is a half-brother

named Philip, who is intellectually disabled and cannot rule.

The most powerful man alive has no heir. So his generals crowd around the bed and ask the only question left. Who gets the empire?

And as the story goes, Alexander gives that final, fatal answer. To the strongest. Now, historians are not even sure he said

it. Some sources say he was already past speaking, and simply pressed his signet ring into the hand of a general named Perdiccas.

But whether he said the words or not barely matters. Because the strongest is exactly who fought for it. Alexander's body is barely

cold when the carving begins. Within days, at a meeting called the Partition of Babylon, the generals slice up the empire like a map spread

across a dinner table. Ptolemy grabs Egypt. Lysimachus takes Thrace. Antigonus seizes a chunk of Asia.

Perdiccas rules as regent for two puppet kings. The unborn baby, and the disabled brother. For a moment, they pretend it is still one empire.

It is not. They turn on each other. For over forty years, Alexander's best friends and finest generals, the men who conquered the world side by side, hunt and kill each other across it.

History calls them the Diadochi. The Successors.

And then they do something colder than any battle. They erase the bloodline. Alexander's half-brother, the puppet king, is executed.

And around three hundred ten BC, his young son and his widow Roxana, remember her, are quietly murdered in secret.

Within about thirteen years of Alexander's death, his entire family is gone. Deliberately wiped out. The empire he built to last forever could not outlive

one single man. But here is the twist.

Not everything he built died with him. The wreckage finally settles into three great kingdoms. Ptolemy's Egypt. The Seleucid Empire in the east. And Antigonid Macedon.

And even as the generals fought, something spread out of the ruins. Greek language. Greek cities. Greek art and ideas, carried all the way from Egypt to the edge of India.

We call it the Hellenistic Age. And it lasted for three hundred years.

And that name from the beginning, Alexandria, grew into the greatest city of the ancient world. Home to a library that tried to hold the sum of human knowledge. Even Alexander's body became a prize.

Ptolemy stole the corpse, carried it to Egypt, and turned it into a shrine. Roman emperors would come just to stand at his tomb.

Think about that. His empire fell apart in front of his own generals. But the man himself, they worshipped. So here is the strange

truth of Alexander the Great. He built the largest empire the world had yet seen. And it survived him by barely two years.

He is the ultimate proof that conquering the world is one thing, and keeping it is another thing entirely. He mastered the first, and he never even attempted

the second. The most powerful man on earth had three words for

who should inherit it all. To the strongest. And in the end, that turned out to be no one. And that is the part that stays with me. We hand out the word great

for what a person can take. But the skill that actually decides whether any of it lasts, Alexander never even tried to learn. Next time on

Great Empires of History, we leave the world-conquerors behind and walk into one ordinary Roman town, living quietly in the shadow of a mountain.

A city that had no idea it was living on borrowed time. This is Pompeii, and the day the sky turned to fire.

Subscribe, and come with us. We are telling the whole rise and fall of the ancient world, one empire at a time. The strongest survived.

The story did not have to.

## The Persian Empire vs "300": How Much Was Actually True?

URL: https://doodlehistory.com/episodes/persia/
Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_o_2ov3Hskc
Published: 2026-08-20 · Length: 13 min

The Persian Empire once ruled nearly half of humanity — then got flipped. This is the full history of the Achaemenid Persian Empire: how Cyrus the Great, a minor vassal, built the largest empire the world had ever seen, and how it was remembered as the villain by the Greeks who finally beat it.

The Persian Empire explained, from Cyrus the Great to the fall of the Achaemenid dynasty. How did the Persian Empire rise and fall? We follow Cyrus, Cambyses, Darius the Great and Xerxes through the conquest of Babylon and Lydia, the Royal Road and the satrapies, the gold daric, and the Greco-Persian Wars at Marathon, Thermopylae and Salamis — up to Alexander the Great's conquest at Gaugamela and the burning of Persepolis. Was ancient Persia really history's cruelest empire, or just the empire whose enemies wrote the story? A military history of the ancient world: the Achaemenid armies, Marathon and Thermopylae, and the empire that stretched from Egypt to India.

Transcript:

You already know one word from this story: marathon. And it's named for the day a single, outnumbered city shattered a piece of the largest empire the world had ever seen.

That empire ruled, by some estimates, nearly one in two human beings alive on Earth. So how does a giant like that get flipped by a few thousand

farmers? Stick around, because that same flip happens again and again, right up to a king watching his fleet die from a chair on a beach.

Here's what I can't get past. Almost everything we picture when we hear the word Persia was written by the Greeks who beat it. So history's most tolerant empire got remembered as the villain. But to see how it all flipped, you have to go

back to the start. Persia did not rise by being the strongest. It rose by flipping stronger empires, one after another. That is the pattern, all the way to the end. The flipper always becomes the flipped.

Let's rewind two hundred years. Start with a nobody. A minor king in a rugged place called Anshan, tucked in the hills of what is now Iran.

His name is Cyrus. His little kingdom answers to a bigger one, the Medes. Cyrus is a vassal. A servant king who bows to an overlord named Astyages.

Around five hundred fifty-three BC, Cyrus stops bowing. He rebels. Astyages does what any furious overlord would do. He raises his army and marches out to crush the upstart.

And here is where it gets strange. The Median army does not fight for their own king. They mutiny. They seize Astyages, put him in chains, and hand him over to Cyrus. The underdog wins his war without really winning a battle. His enemy's own soldiers handed him a throne.

Cyrus could have executed the captured king. He does not. He spares him. He folds the Medes into his new Persian state instead of burning it down. That mercy becomes his signature.

Now watch the underdog turn into the giant. He marches west to Lydia and its king Croesus, a man so rich we still say

"rich as Croesus." Cyrus storms his capital after a siege of only roughly two weeks. The wealthiest king in the world, gone.

Then the big one. Babylon. The greatest city on Earth. In five hundred thirty-nine BC, Cyrus defeats its army and walks into Babylon, by many accounts almost without a fight. Stop and count the score.

In under twenty years, a vassal nobody has built the largest empire the world has ever seen. From the Aegean coast to the deserts of Central Asia.

But it gets stranger, because of what this conqueror does next. When Cyrus takes Babylon, he does something rare for a conqueror.

He lets captured peoples go home. He returns the gods and temple statues that Babylon's kings had carried off. That policy of return is carved onto

a baked-clay barrel we call the Cyrus Cylinder, dug up in Babylon in eighteen seventy-nine, now sitting in the British Museum. And you will hear that cylinder called "the world's first charter of human rights." It isn't.

That's a myth. The cylinder names peoples east of the Tigris, not some grand universal freedom. And that famous translation floating around

online, the one stuffed with modern human-rights language, historians say that version is basically a fabrication. But here is what is real.

Among the peoples Cyrus let go home were the Judean exiles, held in Babylon for decades. He let them return to Jerusalem and rebuild their Temple.

The Hebrew Bible never forgot it. Isaiah even calls Cyrus God's "anointed," the only non-Jew ever given that title.

His tolerance was genuine. He let conquered peoples keep their gods, their laws, their customs. That is why an empire of so many nations held together. Not the myth. The mercy. Cyrus died

around five hundred thirty BC, fighting nomads on the wild northeastern frontier. By Herodotus's account, he fell to a warrior queen named Tomyris.

They buried the man who ruled the world in a plain stone tomb at Pasargadae. It still stands today. Small. Simple. Alone on an empty plain. Cyrus built the empire.

Now someone had to run it. His son Cambyses added Egypt.

Then, in five hundred twenty-two BC, after a bloody scramble for the crown, a new king seized power. Darius. If Cyrus was the sword,

Darius was the blueprint. He carved the whole empire into about twenty provinces called satrapies. Each one run by a governor, a

satrap. But Darius did not trust his satraps. So he planted watchers in every province, travelling inspectors the Persians called the eyes and ears of the king. Then he built a road.

The Royal Road. Roughly twenty-seven hundred kilometers of it, from Susa to Sardis, with over a hundred stations, each stocked with fresh

horses. A message that took three months on foot could now cross the empire in about a week. Royal couriers rode in relay, day and night, through any weather.

Herodotus wrote about those riders. And his words outlived his empire. "Neither snow, nor rain, nor heat, nor gloom of night."

Sound familiar? It is stamped on post offices today. It was written about Persian messengers two and a half thousand years ago.

Darius wanted money that worked everywhere too. So he minted the gold daric, a thick coin of nearly pure gold, one of the first reliable imperial currencies in history. And he built a palace to show it all off.

Persepolis. Its grand staircase is carved with long lines of people from every corner of the empire, each bringing tribute to the king.

Because the reach was staggering now. Persian records described an empire that ran, in their words, "from India to Ethiopia." From the edge of India across to Egypt and Libya, all the way to the coast of

Greece. Here is a number to sit with. By some estimates, around four hundred eighty BC, as much as roughly forty-four percent of every human being alive on Earth lived under Persian rule. Nearly one in two people on the

planet. By some accounts, no empire before or since has ever held a bigger share of humanity. This was the superpower.

Unbeatable. Its elite guard were called the Immortals. By some accounts, the unit was kept at exactly ten thousand men.

Every soldier who fell was instantly replaced, so the ranks never seemed to shrink. To their enemies, they looked like men who could not die.

So who on Earth could flip a machine like this? A few thousand farmers on the far side of the sea. It starts small. Some Greek cities on the empire's

western edge revolt, and Athens sends help. Darius is insulted. In four hundred ninety BC he ships an army across the Aegean to punish one single city.

Athens. They land on a plain called Marathon. The Athenians are badly outnumbered. They charge anyway. And they do not just win. They shatter the Persians.

By Herodotus's count, six thousand four hundred Persians died on that beach, against just one hundred and ninety-two Athenians. A single city had routed

a piece of the largest empire on Earth. A runner supposedly carried the news home to Athens, and gave us the word "marathon."

Darius wanted revenge. He died before he could take it. So his son inherited the grudge. Xerxes.

In four hundred eighty BC, Xerxes came back, not to punish one city, but to swallow Greece whole. He came with an army so vast that Herodotus

claimed it numbered in the millions. Modern historians think that figure is wildly exaggerated. But it was still one of the largest forces the ancient

world ever gathered. The Greeks tried to hold him at a narrow mountain pass. Thermopylae. And here is the part nobody tells you.

You have heard it was three hundred Spartans against the whole Persian army. That is the movie version. The truth is bigger. About seven thousand Greeks held

that pass together, for days. Not three hundred. Seven thousand. The three hundred come only at the very end.

A local traitor showed the Persians a hidden mountain path and guided them around behind the Greeks. Most of the army retreated to fight another day.

And to cover them, about three hundred Spartans, plus roughly seven hundred Thespians nobody ever names, stayed behind to die. And they did.

Thermopylae was a Persian victory. But it cost them time. And it turned the Greeks into legends. Then came the sea.

Which brings us right back to that throne on the beach. Xerxes' fleet chased the Greek ships into the tight strait of Salamis. The Athenian commander Themistocles had lured them in on purpose. In open water, Persia's huge

numbers were a weapon. Crammed into a narrow channel, those same numbers became a trap. Ships crashed into ships.

No room to turn. Xerxes watched from his throne on the shore, waiting for a slaughter. He got one. His own. By ancient accounts,

Persia lost on the order of two to three hundred ships that day. The Greeks lost around forty. The king who came to devour Greece pulled

his army out and went home. The next year, in four hundred seventy-nine BC, the Greeks destroyed the last Persian force left behind, at Plataea. The invasion of mainland Greece was over.

And here is where you would expect the story to end. The superpower humbled. The empire falls. Except it didn't.

Losing Greece barely scratched Persia. Greece was a distant fringe, an edge of the map. The empire lived on for roughly another hundred and fifty years.

Cyrus's machine was that strong. But it rotted from the inside. Satraps rebelled against the throne. Kings were poisoned and stabbed by their own families.

The court became a nest of intrigue and murder. The sword that conquered the world slowly turned on itself.

And then a new underdog appeared. From the north. From a rough kingdom the Persians barely respected. Macedon.

His name was Alexander. In three hundred thirty-four BC, Alexander crossed into Asia with a small, ferocious army. At a river called the Granicus, he smashed the first Persian force sent to stop him.

Asia Minor cracked open. The next year, at Issus, he met the Great King himself, Darius the Third. And Darius did something that would

stain his name forever. When the battle turned against him, he ran. He fled his own chariot and abandoned his mother, his wife, and his children in the camp. Alexander captured all of them.

Then, on the first of October, three hundred thirty-one BC, the two kings faced each other one last time. Gaugamela.

Darius had the far bigger army. Alexander had roughly forty thousand men. It did not matter. Alexander drove a cavalry charge straight at the Persian

center, aimed at the Great King himself. And once again, Darius ran. The heart of the empire was gone.

Alexander took Babylon. He took Susa. And he took Persepolis, Darius the Great's shining palace of a hundred

nations. And then Persepolis burned. Why is still argued to this day. Some ancient writers say it

was a drunken revel, a fire started on a dare by a courtesan named Thais. Others say it was cold revenge, payback for the day

Xerxes had burned Athens. Either way, the greatest palace of the ancient world went up in flames. Darius the Third never saw the true

end. Fleeing east, beaten and desperate, he was stabbed to death. Not by Alexander, but by one of his own satraps, a man named Bessus,

who wanted the crown for himself. That was it. After roughly two hundred and twenty years,

the Achaemenid dynasty was over. Its last king murdered by his own governor, dying in the dirt by the roadside.

The flipper had become the flipped. But an empire that big does not simply vanish. It leaves a blueprint. Alexander did not tear Persia's system down.

He kept it. The satrapies, the roads, the couriers, the coins, the whole idea of ruling many peoples under one crown. His successors borrowed it, and in time, so did Rome.

And it is still around you. The marathon race is named for a battle against Persia. The postal line about snow and rain and gloom of night was written about Persian

riders. Provincial governors, kept honest by inspectors, that idea is Persian too. It is sitting quietly in the shape of the world you live in

right now. And Cyrus, the underdog who started it all, is remembered as something rarer than a conqueror. As a liberator.

The king who let the captives go home. An empire that ruled nearly half of humanity. Begun by a vassal whose own enemy handed him a throne. Ended by a king who watched his navy die from a chair on the beach.

The real lesson of Persia is not how high it rose. It is that the ones who flip giants become giants, and giants, in

the end, always get flipped. And here is the part I can't shake. We only know this empire through the people who beat it.

The most tolerant power of the ancient world came down to us as the villain in someone else's story. History does not belong to the strongest.

It belongs to whoever survives to tell it. And Persia lost the story long before it lost the war. Next time, we follow the man who finished

the job. The Macedonian outsider who chased Darius across the world, torched Persepolis, and swallowed the largest empire on Earth before he even

turned thirty. Alexander the Great, the man who would finish what Greece started and take Persia whole. Subscribe, and I will see you there.

## Did the Vikings Really Disappear in 1066?

URL: https://doodlehistory.com/episodes/vikings/
Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1qMzYeFkGEQ
Published: 2026-08-13 · Length: 12 min

Everyone says the Vikings vanished in one bloody week in 1066. They didn't — they won, wearing a new name. This is the real story of the Viking Age (793–1066): the raids, the longships, the voyage to America 471 years before Columbus, and the twist that the men who "ended" the Vikings were Vikings themselves.

The Vikings, explained. Who the Vikings really were, why the Viking Age began with the raid on Lindisfarne in 793, how the Great Heathen Army nearly swallowed England, and why it "ended" at Stamford Bridge and Hastings in 1066. We cover Harald Hardrada, Alfred the Great and the Danelaw, Rollo and Normandy, Erik the Red and Leif Erikson reaching Vinland (North America) in 1021, Cnut the Great's North Sea empire, and Harald Bluetooth — plus how the Normans, and every English monarch since, carry Viking blood. And the myths: no, they never wore horned helmets, and yes, you still speak dozens of their words and name four days of your week after their gods. A military and social history of the Viking Age: the raids from Lindisfarne to 1066, the settlements from Greenland to North America, and the archaeology behind the myths.

Transcript:

You speak Viking every single day, and you have no idea. Sky, egg, knife, window, husband: every one of those words is Old Norse, left behind by the most feared raiders in history.

Four days of your week are named after their gods, and even the Bluetooth in your phone is a dead Viking king's initials. Everyone says these people vanished

a thousand years ago, in one bloody week in ten sixty-six, so why won't they get out of your Tuesday? Here's my take, and it's the whole reason

I made this. The Vikings never vanished. They lost their ships and their gods, and then they did something sneakier: they moved in. By the end of this, you won't

see them as ancient history. You'll realize you've been carrying them your whole life. But here's the strange part.

The man who won that week, the man history calls a Norman, was secretly a Viking himself. So the people who supposedly ended the Viking Age were Vikings. Hold onto that.

It's the twist this whole story turns on. Now picture the week. A Norwegian giant named Harald Hardrada lands in northern England with a war fleet. Men call him the last great Viking, and they are not exaggerating.

On the twenty-fifth of September, the English king, Harold Godwinson, catches him at a river crossing called Stamford Bridge. It is a slaughter.

Hardrada is cut down, by some accounts an arrow through the throat. The Norwegian invasion dies with him in the mud.

England has just crushed the Vikings. Three hundred years of terror, over in an afternoon. Except it isn't.

Nineteen days later, a third king lands in the south. Harold, exhausted and bleeding, turns his army around and marches the whole length of England to meet him. The place is called Hastings.

And on the fourteenth of October, Harold loses everything. His army. His crown. His life. So did the Vikings really end in

ten sixty-six? Or did they just win, wearing a new name?

To answer that, we rewind almost three hundred years, to a quiet island, on a summer morning, when the whole nightmare began. The eighth of June, seven hundred ninety-three. Off the northern coast of England sits a tiny island called Lindisfarne.

On it, a monastery. One of the holiest places in Christian Europe, the shrine of Saint Cuthbert, full of gold and silver and unarmed monks.

That morning, sails appear on the horizon. The men who come ashore are like nothing Europe has seen. They do not come to trade or settle.

They kill the monks, snatch the treasure, seize prisoners to sell, and vanish back out to sea before anyone can stop them.

A scholar named Alcuin was horrified. He wrote that the church of Saint Cuthbert was spattered with the blood of the priests of God. Nobody even had a word for these

raiders yet. The Franks called them Northmen. But history remembers them by the Old Norse word for what they did out on the water.

Viking. To go raiding. Say the word Viking, and you probably picture a giant in a horned helmet. Drop that image right now.

Because no horned Viking helmet has ever been found. Not one. In over a thousand graves, in every dig, nothing

with horns. The only near-complete Viking helmet we have ever dug up, from a place called Gjermundbu in Norway, is a plain, rounded iron cap. So where did the horns come from?

A costume designer. In the year eighteen seventy-six, for a German opera by Richard Wagner. Somebody drew horns on the singers, and the world never let go. The scariest warriors in history are famous for

a hat they never wore. They were not filthy barbarians either. Their graves are full of combs and tweezers, and English writers complained the Danes

bathed too often and dressed too well. And they were not one nation, but three separate, often rival kingdoms, Norway, Denmark, and Sweden, who raided each other as happily as everyone else. Most Norse never raided at all.

They were farmers, traders, and poets. So what turned a handful of these farmers into the terror of Europe? One invention.

The longship. A long, low boat of overlapping oak planks, light enough to cross open ocean and then row straight up a river into your town.

No compass, no maps. They steered by the sun, the stars, and the flight of birds. And when those sails came over the horizon, there was nowhere far enough inland

to be safe. For decades, it stayed hit-and-run. Raid a monastery, burn a village, sail home rich.

But in the year eight hundred sixty-five, that changed. The Vikings stopped visiting. They came to stay. A huge coalition landed in England,

remembered as the Great Heathen Army. By legend, it was led by the sons of a Viking hero named Ragnar Lothbrok, come to avenge their father.

But be careful here. Most historians think Ragnar never existed as one real man, that he is a legend stitched together from several different warriors. His supposed sons, though, were real enough, and they were coming

for a kingdom. This army rolled over England. It took the city of York. It toppled the north. One by one, the old English kingdoms fell, until only one was left standing.

Wessex. And its young king, Alfred. Alfred lost battles. He paid the Vikings to leave.

At his lowest point, he was hiding in a swamp. And then, in eight hundred seventy-eight, he came back and beat them at a place called Edington.

The peace that followed split England in two. The north and east became the Danelaw, land under Viking law, Viking words, Viking names.

To this day, if an English town ends in "by," a Viking named it. Meanwhile, across the water in France, other

Vikings were doing the same to the Franks. Sailing up the Seine. Besieging Paris. Refusing to leave.

So in the year nine hundred eleven, the French king tried something desperate. He gave up. He handed a Viking chieftain named Rollo a whole province, if only he would guard the coast and stop the raids.

The land took its name from those Northmen. Normandy. Remember that name. Remember Rollo. We are going to need him at the end.

Now here is the part nobody tells you. While half the Norse world was busy conquering, the other half was doing something no European had ever done.

They were sailing off the edge of the map. They settled Iceland, empty and volcanic. And there, around the year nine hundred thirty, free

farmers founded something astonishing. A parliament. The Althing. One of the oldest law-assemblies on Earth, and it still

meets today. From Iceland, an exile named Erik the Red pushed west, to a frozen island he cleverly sold as Greenland to lure

settlers in. And from Greenland, his son sailed further still. His name was Leif Erikson. And around the year ten hundred,

Leif's ships reached a green, wooded shore full of wild grapes. He called it Vinland. Wine-land. It was North America. Let that land. Vikings stood in the New World.

For centuries that was just a story in an old saga, until nineteen sixty-one, when archaeologists found their actual camp. Turf-walled halls, on the tip of Newfoundland, at a place called L'Anse aux Meadows.

The real thing. But it gets better. In twenty twenty-one, scientists worked out the exact year the Vikings were there. Here is how.

In the year nine hundred ninety-three, a huge solar storm struck the Earth and left a chemical fingerprint in every living tree. The Vikings cut their camp's timber with metal

tools. And three of those beams carried that nine hundred ninety-three marker, plus exactly twenty-eight rings grown after it. Do the math.

The Vikings were standing in America in the year ten twenty-one. That is four hundred and seventy-one years before Columbus ever set sail.

And they were not only going west. Swedish Vikings turned east, down the great rivers of what is now Russia, a country that takes its name from them, the Rus. They traded furs and slaves for Arab silver, all

the way to Baghdad. They reached Constantinople, the greatest city on Earth, and the toughest of them guarded the emperor himself, as his elite bodyguard.

Keep that bodyguard in mind. One of them is about to come home and change everything. Back in the north, the world of the Vikings was quietly ending.

Not by the sword. By the crown, and by the cross. The age of a thousand sea-raiders was giving way to a few strong kings.

In Norway, a ruler remembered as Harald Fairhair is said to have united the country after a great sea-battle, by tradition around

the year eight hundred seventy-two. Though historians dispute that date, and see the real unification as a slow grind over generations, not one

clean victory. In Denmark, a king with an unforgettable name, Harald Bluetooth, raised a giant carved stone that named Denmark for the very first time, and boasted that he had made the Danes Christian.

Yes. That Bluetooth. The wireless tech in your phone is named after him. Its logo is literally his initials, written in Viking runes.

And as the Norse became Christian, the raiding culture that once worshipped Odin and Thor began to burn out from the inside. Kings do not plunder churches.

They build them. But before the Vikings faded, one of them pulled off something staggering. Harald Bluetooth's grandson was a man named Cnut.

And Cnut the Great did not just raid England. He conquered it, and crowned himself king. Then he took Denmark.

Then Norway. One Viking, ruling a North Sea empire, from three thrones at once. There is a famous story about him.

His flatterers said he was so mighty even the sea would obey him. So he set his throne on the beach and ordered the tide to stop. It did not. The water soaked his royal feet. That was the point.

Even a king is powerless before God. And no empire, however great, lasts forever. Cnut's died with his sons.

Which brings us right back to where we started. The autumn of ten sixty-six. Three men wanted England. The first was Harold Godwinson, the English king,

crowned that January. The second was Harald Hardrada of Norway. Remember him? The Viking who had served in Constantinople and come home hungry for a throne, who believed England was his, and sailed to take

it. That is the battle we opened with. Stamford Bridge. The forced march, the ambush, the last great Viking dead in the English mud. It looked like total victory. And then the sails appeared in the south.

The third man was William, Duke of Normandy. And here, finally, is the answer to the question I asked you at the very beginning. Normandy.

Land of the Northmen. William was the great-great-great-grandson of Rollo, the very Viking raider France had handed that coast to back in nine hundred eleven.

His ancestors were the same men who once terrorized the Seine. He spoke French now. He fought on horseback now. But his blood was Norse.

So look at what really happened in ten sixty-six. A Viking king of Norway invaded England, and lost. And a Viking king's descendant invaded England, and won.

Both sides of Hastings could trace their swords back to the longship. The Vikings did not lose in ten sixty-six. That is the twist.

They beat themselves. And then one branch of them took the English crown and never handed it back. Every king and queen of England since sits on a throne a

Viking's great-grandson seized at Hastings. So the age that began with blood on a monastery floor ended in a field near Hastings.

But the Vikings never really left. They just got quieter.

Look at your own week. Four of your days are named after Norse gods. Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday, Friday. Thursday is literally Thor's

day. Listen to yourself talk. When you say sky, egg, knife, window, husband, or law, you are speaking Old Norse, words the Vikings left behind in England. Even the words they and them are theirs.

They named towns you can still visit. York, Dublin, Grimsby, Whitby. They gave Russia its name. They built one of the world's first parliaments, still sitting in Iceland. America even keeps a holiday for Leif Erikson, every

ninth of October. And that's the part that stays with me. The Vikings didn't end in a field near Hastings. They just went quiet, hiding in your words, your week, and your kings. You didn't just learn about them today.

You inherited them. So next time you picture a Viking in a horned helmet, remember, that helmet is a costume from an opera. The real Vikings were stranger, and far bigger, than the cartoon. They reached America five centuries

early. And in one wild week of ten sixty-six, they lost England to the terror of the sea-kings, and won it back with a sea-king's own grandson.

Three kings, two battles, one arrow. And the men who ended the Viking Age were Vikings all along. If that rewired how you see history,

you will want to be here for the next one. Because we are leaving the cold northern seas for the golden heart of the ancient world. The Persian Empire. The superpower of its age, ruled by a man who called himself King of Kings.

Subscribe, and I will see you there. The nightmare that began on one quiet island ended with a crown. Funny, how history loops.

## How Did the Inca Empire Lose to Just 168 Men?

URL: https://doodlehistory.com/episodes/inca/
Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Pc-ktJ0Nqwo
Published: 2026-08-06 · Length: 11 min

The Inca Empire was the largest state the Americas ever built — around ten million people, forty thousand kilometres of mountain road, no wheel and no writing — yet it fell to fewer than two hundred Spaniards in barely a year. This is the real history of how the Inca Empire didn't so much get conquered as collapse from the inside.

How did the Inca Empire fall so fast? Here is the Inca Empire explained end to end: the rise of Tawantinsuyu under Pachacuti, the god-emperor system of the Sapa Inca, the smallpox epidemic that killed Huayna Capac and triggered the civil war between Atahualpa and Huascar, and the Battle of Cajamarca in 1532, where Francisco Pizarro captured the emperor Atahualpa. We cover the Atahualpa ransom and the room of gold, his execution in 1533, the Spanish conquest of Peru, and the last Inca holdout at Vilcabamba until 1572. A history of Andean civilization: the Inca armies and roads, the Spanish conquest that began at Cajamarca, and an empire administered without writing or the wheel.

Chapters:
  0:00 The conquistador who carried no sword
  0:54 The impossible empire
  2:52 Ruled by a god: the fatal flaw
  3:51 The invisible invader
  5:09 Brother against brother
  6:38 Cajamarca: the god is captured
  8:28 The room of gold
  10:26 Why it really fell

Transcript:

The deadliest conquistador in history never carried a sword. It reached the Inca years before the Spanish did. It raced up their own mountain roads, faster than any army, and walked straight into the palace.

By the time Pizarro's hundred and sixty-eight men showed up, this invisible killer had already murdered the emperor, killed his heir, and set brother against brother.

So the Spanish did not conquer the largest empire in the Americas. They looted a body that was already dying. Here's what I actually believe.

The Inca were never really conquered. They were caught in the middle of destroying themselves, and Pizarro just happened to be standing there to take the credit.

So play the what-if with me. If that self-inflicted wound had never happened, Pizarro walks into a united empire of millions and

gets crushed. That is the whole story. Let me show you how an empire

this powerful got that fragile. First, you need to feel how impossible this fall really was. This empire had a name.

Tawantinsuyu. It means the Land of the Four Parts. Four great quarters, all meeting at one sacred city, Cusco.

Picture the scale. By most estimates, ten to twelve million people.

About two million square kilometers of land. It ran the length of the Andes, roughly five and a half thousand kilometers, north to south.

Now here is the part that breaks your brain. They did all of this with no wheel. No wheeled cart anywhere in the empire. They did it with no horses.

The only pack animal was the llama, plus human backs.

And they did it with no writing. None. No books, no letters, no alphabet. So how do you run ten million people with no writing?

You tie knots. They kept their records on the quipu. Knotted, colored cords. A hanging string could hold a number, a census, a tax owed. An accountant read the knots with his fingers.

And the roads. Oh, the roads. Over forty thousand kilometers of stone highway threaded through the mountains.

Runners sprinted the route in relays, handing off to a fresh runner every few kilometers, carrying messages, and even fresh fish from the coast, up into

the peaks. Every subject owed the state labor instead of money. Build this road. Farm this terrace. March in this army.

And whole villages could be picked up and moved wherever the empire wanted them.

Here is the twist that makes the fall so shocking. This giant was young. Very young. For most of its life, Cusco

was just a small mountain kingdom. Then, starting around fourteen thirty-eight, one ruler, Pachacuti, whose name meant Shaker of the World, began swallowing

his neighbors whole. From little kingdom to continental empire in under a hundred years. So this was not some ancient, exhausted state.

It was fresh, sharp, and expanding. Which makes what happened next feel impossible. Unless you know the hidden crack running right through the middle of it.

Here is the crack. And it is everything. The Inca were not ruled by a king. They were ruled by a god.

The Sapa Inca, the Sole Inca, was believed to be a living descendant of Inti, the sun itself. Not a man chosen by the sun. The sun's blood, walking the earth. Every law, every army, every harvest

flowed through his one sacred body. And when a Sapa Inca died? He didn't really leave. His mummy kept his palaces, his servants, his gold. They dressed him, fed him, and paraded him at festivals.

The dead emperors still owned their wealth. Which meant each new emperor inherited the throne, but not the treasure. So he had to go conquer his own. A built-in engine for endless war. But look closely at that god-king setup,

because it hides a fatal flaw. The whole empire ran through one person. One sacred man was the state. So what happens to a machine like that if you seize the one man at the center?

Hold that thought. It is the hinge everything turns on.

Now the empire was strong. The empire was organized. And then something invisible came over the mountains and started killing.

Here is the part almost nobody tells you about the Spanish conquest. Remember that swordless killer I opened with? It is time to name it.

A disease. Smallpox. An Old World killer the Andes had never met. And it did something eerie.

It arrived before the Spanish did. It raced ahead of the invaders, jumping village to village through native trade routes, running up the very roads the Inca built. Faster than any army. Around fifteen twenty-seven, it reached

the heart of the empire. And it walked straight into the palace.

The emperor at the time was Huayna Capac, who had pushed the empire to its greatest size. Around fifteen twenty-seven, an Old World epidemic, most likely smallpox, killed him.

That alone would have been a crisis. But the plague wasn't finished. The heir he had named, his chosen successor, caught the same disease and

died before he could ever take the throne. Two deaths. The god-king and his heir, gone in a season.

And a throne with no clear owner. Now remember, this was a god-emperor empire built to obey one sacred person. Take that person away with

no successor, and you don't get a smooth handover. You get a war. Two of Huayna Capac's sons reached for the empty throne.

Atahualpa, in the north, backed by the hardened army of Quito. And Huascar, crowned in the sacred capital of Cusco.

Brother against brother. For roughly three years, the empire turned its incredible war machine inward and used it on itself.

This is the War of the Two Brothers. Cities burned. Armies clashed. The road runners now carried news of Inca killing Inca.

And whole peoples who had been conquered by the Inca watched their masters bleed, and quietly remembered every cruelty. Then, around fifteen thirty-two,

Atahualpa's generals won. They captured his brother Huascar. Atahualpa was the victor. But think about what that victory looked like.

He had won an empire that was bloodied, split down the middle, its elite freshly divided into winners and losers, its subject peoples seething. He had won a broken thing.

And at that exact moment, on the coast, a small group of strangers on enormous animals were marching inland. The timing is

almost too perfect to believe. Now here is your what-if.

If the plague had never come, Huayna Capac lives, the succession is clean, no civil war. Pizarro lands in a calm, united empire of millions and never leaves the coast alive. But that is not what he found.

He found a fresh wound. And he walked his fingers straight into it.

November sixteenth, fifteen thirty-two. The town of Cajamarca. Atahualpa was camped there with a huge army. By some accounts

as many as eighty thousand men. He was the victor, a living

god, utterly unworried. What could a hundred and sixty-eight tired foreigners possibly do to him? He agreed to meet them in the town square.

He came in on a litter, unarmed, surrounded by thousands of unarmed attendants, in his ceremonial finest. Why would a god need weapons?

The Spanish were hidden in the buildings around the plaza. Steel swords. Armor. Guns and a cannon. And around sixty-two horses, animals the Inca had never seen, huge

and terrifying. A priest approached the emperor and handed him a holy book. Atahualpa, from a world with no writing, held the strange object, and threw it to the ground. That was the signal.

The cannon fired. The horses exploded out of the buildings. And in the packed square, the slaughter began.

The Spanish cut through the unarmed crowd around the emperor. The Inca, stunned by the noise, the horses, the steel, were trapped and

cut down. Pizarro drove straight for one target. Atahualpa. He seized the emperor alive, off his litter, in the

middle of his own army. When it was over, the reports say not

a single Spaniard had died. Pizarro's only wound was a cut on the hand, taken while grabbing his prize. And now, remember the crack.

The empire that ran through one sacred man had just lost that man to the enemy.

The tens of thousands of soldiers nearby? They froze. You do not act against the men holding the living son of the sun. Capturing one person had paralyzed a state of millions.

The single point of failure had just failed. Atahualpa, still a captive,

was clever. He saw how these strangers looked at gold. So he made the most astonishing offer in history.

He pointed at the room he was held in. He promised to fill it once with gold, and twice over with silver, in exchange for his freedom. And his empire delivered.

From every temple and palace, treasure came. Gold sun-disks, silver, worked art, all carried in and melted

into bars. By one estimate, something like thirteen thousand pounds of gold and twice that in silver. Often called the largest ransom ever paid.

He paid it in full. And the Spanish took the gold, and killed him anyway. In fifteen thirty-three, on false charges, they condemned him.

To avoid being burned, he accepted baptism, and was strangled instead. The last emperor of the united empire was gone. So, was it really a

hundred and sixty-eight men? No. And this is the honest answer the what-if reveals. It was a stack of disasters, all landing at once.

A plague that killed the emperor and the heir before the Spanish even appeared. A civil war that split the army and the elite. A god-king system with a single point of failure, that Pizarro decapitated in one afternoon.

Steel, horses, and guns against wood and stone.

And this is the part that stings the most. Tens of thousands of the Inca's own subjects joined the invaders. Peoples like the Cañari and the Chachapoya, brutalized under Inca rule, saw the Spanish as the enemy of their enemy.

When the Spanish later fought to hold Cusco, they were defended by more than thirty thousand native allies. And even then it wasn't clean.

A puppet emperor the Spanish installed, Manco Inca, turned on them and rebelled. He fled into the mountains and founded a rebel Inca state at Vilcabamba, which held out for nearly forty years.

Only in fifteen seventy-two did the Spanish storm it and behead the very last Sapa Inca. So the Spanish did not topple the Inca.

The Inca had already half-toppled themselves. The Spanish just lit the match on kindling that was already stacked. Which leaves us with the haunting what-if.

Cancel one thing. Cancel the plague, and there is no civil war.

A united Tawantinsuyu, millions strong, meets a hundred and sixty-eight men, and swallows them without noticing.

The greatest empire in the Americas was not conquered. It was caught at the one moment it had turned its sword on itself.

So no, I don't think Pizarro conquered anything. I think he walked in and took

the credit for a suicide already in progress. An empire is never really killed from the outside first. It is cracked from the inside, and then the

outsider only has to push. If you want to keep walking through the empires that broke this way, subscribe and stay with the series.

Because the next story leaves the mountains of the Andes entirely, and sails cold northern seas, with men who turned raiding into an empire of their own. That one is coming next.

## What Really Destroyed the Aztec Empire? (Not Spain)

URL: https://doodlehistory.com/episodes/aztec-empire/
Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=drw7GZzwW8k
Published: 2026-07-30 · Length: 13 min

The Aztec Empire built the biggest city in the Americas and ruled several million people, then fell in just two years. But the story that a few hundred Spaniards toppled it is a myth. This is the real history of the rise and fall of the Aztec Empire, and what really destroyed it.

How did the Aztec Empire fall? The Aztecs, or Mexica, founded Tenochtitlan on a lake around 1325, forged the Triple Alliance in 1428 under Itzcoatl and Tlacaelel, and built a vast tribute empire crowned by the Templo Mayor. This is the Aztec Empire explained: the truth about human sacrifice, Moctezuma the Second, Hernan Cortes and Malintzin, the Tlaxcalan alliance, the smallpox epidemic, and the 93-day siege that ended with the fall of Tenochtitlan on 13 August 1521 — a conquest won by the Aztecs' own indigenous enemies, disease, and Spanish steel, not by a handful of conquistadors. A history of Mesoamerican civilization and conquest: Tenochtitlan's rise from a swamp, the war with Cortés, and the archaeology of the skull tower that revised the story.

  0:00 The Myth
  0:44 A People Nobody Wanted
  1:46 From Vassals to Masters
  2:57 The Tribute Machine
  4:25 The Temple and the Sacrifice Myth
  6:04 The Strangers Arrive
  8:13 Inside the City: Hostage and the Night of Sorrows
  9:45 The Invisible Killer and the Fall

Transcript:

You already know the story they told you. A few hundred Spaniards sailed in and toppled an empire of millions. It sounds impossible. And here is the twist. It is impossible, because it never actually happened

that way. Here is what I think really happened. The Aztecs did not lose to strangers. They lost to the empire they had already

built. The truth is far stranger than the legend, and I can prove

it with numbers. This was the biggest city in the Americas, and it vanished in just two years. An empire of several million people, gone in the

time it takes to grow a garden. And I can show you exactly who really destroyed it. Tens of thousands of the Aztecs' own neighbors, the enemies they had spent

a century making. So let me rewind, all the way back to a swamp. Start with a wandering people nobody wanted.

They called themselves the Mexica, and everyone around them looked down on them. They had no land, no city, and no home of their own.

They survived by fighting other people's wars as hired soldiers. They were the poor, warlike outsiders that better-off cities used and despised.

But they carried a promise from their god, Huitzilopochtli, the god of the sun and war. He told them to wander until they saw a sign.

An eagle, perched on a prickly-pear cactus. By tradition, around the year thirteen twenty-five, on a marshy island in Lake Texcoco, they saw it. An eagle, standing on a cactus, exactly as promised.

So on that useless little island, in the middle of a lake, they built a city. They called it Tenochtitlan.

And here is the first thing nobody tells you. They did not build their capital on the best land. They built it on the worst land, land nobody else even wanted.

Which raises the obvious question. How does the poorest people in the valley end

up ruling all of it? For about a hundred years, they did not rule anything. The Mexica were still vassals, servants of a powerful city called Azcapotzalco. They fought its battles, and they paid it tribute, year after year. They were the muscle, and someone else took the reward.

Then, in the fourteen twenties, everything flipped.

A king named Itzcoatl took the throne of Tenochtitlan. Beside him stood one of the most important men most people have never heard

of. His name was Tlacaelel, and he was never king. He was the cihuacoatl, which we can loosely call the prime minister. He ran the finances, planned the wars, and appointed the generals. He was the second most powerful man in the empire, and he stayed in the shadows for

decades. Together, Itzcoatl and Tlacaelel did the unthinkable. They rose up and crushed their own masters at Azcapotzalco.

Then, in fourteen twenty-eight, they formed an alliance with two other cities, Texcoco and Tlacopan. Three cities, bound together, sharing the spoils. Historians call it the Triple Alliance.

And that alliance is the true birth of the Aztec Empire. The despised servants had just become the masters. Now they built a machine, and

it was terrifyingly good at one thing. The Aztec Empire was not really one country, the way you might picture it. It was a tribute empire.

They let conquered cities keep their own kings and their own gods. On one condition. You pay, and you send warriors, forever.

By some accounts, tribute flowed in from hundreds of city-states across dozens of provinces. And what tribute it was.

Gold dust, and jade, and jewelry, poured into the island city. Cotton cloth, and brilliant feathers, and cacao beans, the beans they made

chocolate from. Rubber, and dye, and grain, and chillies, all of it flowing toward the lake. And, of course, prisoners.

But how do you feed a giant city built on a lake? The Mexica had an answer that looks like magic. They farmed the water itself.

They built chinampas, raised garden plots in the shallow lake, so fertile they could grow crops all year. People sometimes call them floating gardens.

Three great causeways connected the island to the shore, with wooden bridges that could be pulled up. A stone aqueduct carried fresh spring water into the heart of the city. Long-distance merchants called the pochteca

traded across the whole region, and secretly, they spied for the empire.

Remember that aqueduct and those causeways. They are going to matter more than

almost anything else in this story. At the center of it all stood a mountain of stone. The Great Temple, the Templo Mayor, rose

roughly sixty meters into the sky. On top sat twin shrines, side by side. One for Huitzilopochtli, the sun and war.

One for Tlaloc, the rain. And this is where we have to talk about the thing everyone thinks they know. Human sacrifice. The Aztecs believed the sun-god needed human blood to keep the sun moving across the sky. Without blood, they

thought, the world would simply stop. So they went to war partly to capture prisoners for the altars. They even fought special, prearranged battles called Flower Wars, against enemies like Tlaxcala, just to take captives

alive. Now, here is the part nobody tells you.

The sacrifice was real, and archaeologists have confirmed it. Near the Great Temple, they dug up a tower of human skulls. Roughly four hundred and fifty skulls, in a single grim structure.

But then there is the famous number, and you have probably heard it. That the Aztecs once sacrificed eighty thousand people in four days.

That figure comes from a Spanish friar, writing generations after the events. And modern scholars think it is wildly exaggerated

propaganda. Do the math. Eighty thousand people in four days means killing more than a dozen human beings every single minute, without ever stopping, day and night.

It is almost certainly impossible. The true number is unknown, and some estimates put it at only a few thousand. So the horror was real,

but the story was stretched, on purpose, by the people who came to conquer them. Hold on to that idea. Because the whole legend of the conquest was stretched the

exact same way. By the year fifteen nineteen, Tenochtitlan was breathtaking. It was one of the largest cities on the entire planet. Perhaps two hundred thousand people or more, likely bigger than most cities in Europe.

Bigger, quite possibly, than London. This was the city at its peak, under a ruler named Moctezuma the Second. And then, on the coast, sails

appeared. The man on those ships was Hernan Cortes.

And now I need you to look very carefully at the numbers, because this is the whole point. Cortes landed with only about five hundred men. Sixteen horses. Eleven ships.

Five hundred men, against an empire of millions.

If the legend were true, this is the moment it should have ended, instantly. So how did five hundred men not simply get swallowed whole?

The answer starts with one person. A woman. Her name was Malintzin, and history sometimes calls her La Malinche. She was a Nahua

woman, handed to the Spanish, and she could speak the local language, Nahuatl, as well as Maya. Suddenly, Cortes could talk.

He could make deals, and threats, and promises. And it turned out a lot of people in this empire had a reason to listen. Because that tribute machine,

all that gold and cloth and prisoners flowing to the lake, it was flowing away from somebody. The very first city Cortes met, the Totonac, were sick of paying the Aztecs. Then Cortes burned his

own ships, so his men could never turn back. And then he found his prize.

The Tlaxcalans. The Tlaxcalans were a fierce people the Aztecs had never conquered. They were the old enemy, the ones the Aztecs hunted in those Flower Wars. At first, they fought Cortes hard.

Then they made a colder calculation. They joined him, against their ancient tormentors. And they did not send a handful of men. They sent thousands. The tiny Spanish band had just become an army.

And to prove how ruthless they now were, at a city called Cholula, Cortes and his Tlaxcalan allies massacred thousands of unarmed people. It was a message, written in blood, aimed straight at the capital.

On the eighth of November, fifteen nineteen, they walked into Tenochtitlan. Cortes, his Spaniards, and about a thousand Tlaxcalan warriors, crossing

that great causeway. Moctezuma the Second came out and received them, peacefully, on the road. And within about a week, Cortes did something staggering.

He seized the emperor inside his own palace. The most powerful man in the Americas, a hostage, in his own home.

For months, Cortes ruled the empire through the captive king.

But it could not hold. While Cortes was away on the coast, his deputy, Pedro de Alvarado, made a catastrophe. During a sacred festival called Toxcatl, Alvarado's men slaughtered Aztec nobles as they danced.

And the city exploded. The whole capital rose up in fury.

Moctezuma the Second died in the chaos. And here the sources genuinely disagree. The Spanish said his own people stoned him for surrendering. The Aztecs said the Spanish killed him. We honestly do not know which is true.

But now the Spanish were trapped, on an island, surrounded by a furious city.

So on the night of the thirtieth of June, fifteen twenty, they ran. They tried to sneak out across the causeways in the dark. And the Aztecs caught them.

It was a massacre on the water. The Spanish lost roughly half their men, most of their horses, and all the treasure they had stolen.

They named that night La Noche Triste. The Night of Sorrows. The empire had won. Cortes was beaten, bleeding, and fleeing for his life.

By every rule of the legend, the story should be over right here. The Aztecs should have won. So why didn't they?

Because something invisible had already slipped into the city.

The Spanish did not just bring steel and horses. They brought a disease the Americas had never seen. Smallpox. The Aztecs had no immunity to it, none at

all. And in the autumn of fifteen twenty, it swept through Tenochtitlan. It killed a huge share of the people.

Diseases like this often killed the strong and the young along with the weak. And it killed the new emperor himself, a ruler named Cuitlahuac,

within weeks of taking the throne. Picture it. The city has just won its greatest victory, driven out the invaders.

And now, from the inside, its people are dying in their homes, faster than anyone can bury them. This was a weapon the Aztecs could never fight.

Not a sword. A germ. A new king rose from the ruins, the last of the line, named Cuauhtemoc. And out beyond the lake, Cortes was rebuilding,

and doing something clever. He had thirteen warships built, in pieces, far away, and carried overland to the lake. Thirteen ships, on a mountain

lake, to control the water the Aztecs had always ruled with canoes.

And beside him now stood the real conquering army. Not five hundred Spaniards. On the order of tens of thousands of native allies, perhaps around a hundred thousand Tlaxcalans and others.

That is the number the legend hides from you. The Aztecs were not defeated by strangers.

They were defeated by their own world, turned against them.

On the twenty-second of May, fifteen twenty-one, the siege began.

The thirteen ships closed off the lake. The huge allied army pressed in along the three causeways. And then they did the one thing that could kill the city.

They found the aqueduct, the one that carried fresh water from the hills. And they cut it. The greatest city in the Americas was left to go

thirsty. For ninety-three days, they fought street by street, house by house. The Aztecs did not break easily. When they captured Spaniards, they

dragged them to the top of the Great Temple. And they sacrificed them there, in full view of the besiegers below. Cortes's own allies watched their friends die

on the altars. But thirst, and disease, and a hundred thousand

enemies do not relent. On the thirteenth of August, fifteen twenty-one, Tenochtitlan fell. Cuauhtemoc, the last emperor, was captured trying to escape

by canoe. And with him, the independent Aztec Empire ended.

The Spanish razed the city to the ground. And on top of its bones, they built a new capital, Mexico City, the one still standing today.

Four years later, Cortes had Cuauhtemoc executed, and the last royal

line was gone. So look at what really happened, one more time. An empire of millions did not fall to a few hundred conquistadors.

It fell to three things, working together. Tens of thousands of its own indigenous

enemies, who finally saw their chance. A smallpox epidemic that gutted the city from within. And Spanish steel, cannon, and thirteen ships on a lake. The strangers lit the match.

But the empire was burned down largely by its own neighbors, and by a disease nobody could see. They spent a century making their neighbors pay, and

bleed, and hate them. And in the end it was those neighbors, not the men from across the sea, who pulled the empire down.

The Aztecs believed they had to feed the sun with blood, or the world would end. In the end, their world ended anyway, in a way they never imagined, and

never could have fought. If a wandering band of outsiders can build the greatest city in the Americas, and lose it all in two years, it makes you wonder how fragile any

empire really is. So subscribe, and stay with the series.

Because there is another empire, another glittering civilization that was

certain it would rule forever. And it too is about to learn how quickly forever can end.

## The Odyssey: How Much of It Was Actually Real?

URL: https://doodlehistory.com/episodes/odyssey/
Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=3ohTa6__OeE
Published: 2026-07-25 · Length: 13 min

Homer's Odyssey is the most famous adventure ever told: a one-eyed giant, a witch who turns men into pigs, a ten-year voyage home. But how much of it was ever real? This is the history behind the myth, where the fairy tale ends and the real Bronze Age begins.

The Odyssey explained, and the true story behind it. We follow Odysseus from Troy through the Cyclops, the Sirens, Scylla and Charybdis, Circe and Calypso to his homecoming in Ithaca, then ask the questions everyone is searching after Christopher Nolan's new film: Is the Odyssey a true story? Was the Trojan War real? Did Troy exist? Who was Homer? We look at Heinrich Schliemann's dig at Hisarlik, Mycenaean Greece and the Linear B tablets, the Late Bronze Age Collapse, and the boar's-tusk helmet that proves a sung poem carried a real memory across five hundred years. Part ancient history, part archaeology: Bronze Age Greece, the excavations at Troy, and how scholars separate Homer's myth from Mycenaean history.
