Transcript:

You used a word from this story today, without noticing. Call a computer virus a Trojan horse. Call a long, hard journey an odyssey. You are quoting a poem almost three thousand years old, one that for four

hundred years nobody wrote down at all. People just sang it, out loud,

from memory. For most of those years, we filed the rest of it under make-believe. A one-eyed giant. A witch who turns men into pigs. A sea crawling with monsters. Then people started digging, and the make-believe

began coming true, one impossible detail at a time.

And now the whole story is back on the biggest screens we can build, in the movie everyone is talking about.

Which brings us to one strange question. How much of this was ever real?

And here is what I love about that question. The honest answer is, we are not sure. And I think that is exactly why a story this old

still refuses to die. Here is a taste of how strange the answer gets.

A glittering hoard of gold, dug out of the ruins of Troy, is real, solid gold. And it is about a thousand years too old to have anything

to do with the war. Hold onto that. A song this old should remember nothing. This one remembered things it had no way of knowing. So let me show you exactly

where the fairy tale ends and the history begins. Start with the story itself.

Odysseus is the king of a small Greek island called Ithaca.

He sails off to fight a war at a city called Troy. That war lasts ten years. Then getting home takes him ten more. Twenty years, gone.

Back home, his wife Penelope waits. His son Telemachus was a baby when he left. He will be a grown man before his father walks back through the

door. The voyage home is where the monsters live.

At his first stop, his men sack a town, then linger to feast. The locals bring reinforcements and cut them down. Lesson one: greed gets you killed. His crew will not learn it. Next, an island of people who

eat a strange lotus flower. One bite, and you forget your home, your family, everything. Odysseus has to drag his own weeping men back to the ships. Then the famous one.

A cave belonging to a one-eyed giant named Polyphemus, a son of the sea-god Poseidon. The giant traps the men inside and eats six of them alive.

So Odysseus gets him drunk on wine. The giant asks his name. Odysseus tells him his name is Nobody. Then they sharpen a stake,

harden the tip in the fire, and drive it into the giant's single eye. Polyphemus screams for help. He screams that Nobody is killing him. So none of the other giants come. That one word is the entire trick.

The men escape tied under the bellies of the giant's rams.

But blinding Poseidon's son is a mistake. The giant prays to his father for revenge, and from now on the sea itself wants

Odysseus dead. A wind-god gives him a leather bag holding every storm at sea, so a gentle breeze can carry him home.

In sight of Ithaca, his crew decide the bag is full of gold. They open it. The storms burst out and blow them all the way back.

Then cannibal giants sink eleven of his twelve ships in a single ambush, spearing his men like fish. Only Odysseus's ship escapes.

Then a goddess-witch named Circe drugs his crew and turns them into pigs. He forces her to change them back, and then stays with her for a year anyway. On Circe's advice, he sails to the very

edge of the Underworld to speak with the dead. There the ghost of a blind prophet named Tiresias, still prophetic in death, warns him what is coming. The crew he will lose. The trouble waiting at home. And one rule above all. Do not touch the cattle of the sun.

Remember that. It matters later. Sailing on, he passes the

Sirens, whose singing lures sailors onto the rocks. He plugs his crew's ears with wax. But he ties himself to the mast, so he alone can hear the song and live. Then a narrow strait

with a monster on each side. On one cliff, a six-headed beast called Scylla. In the water, a whirlpool called Charybdis that swallows the sea.

He must choose. He steers close to Scylla, and she snatches six men, one for each head. Then his starving crew make the last mistake.

They kill and eat the sacred cattle of the sun. The warning, ignored. A storm smashes the ship and drowns every last

man but Odysseus. He washes up on the island of a nymph called Calypso, who offers to make him immortal if he stays. He stays about seven years, and cries for home every single day. Finally a kind seafaring people ferry

the broken king home to Ithaca, twenty years after he left. And here the poem turns cold. Odysseus does not march home

a hero. He sneaks in, disguised as a filthy old beggar.

His house is full of men, by some accounts a hundred and eight of them, eating his food and pressuring his wife to remarry. Penelope has been holding them

off with a trick. She promised to choose a husband once she finished weaving a burial shroud. Every day she weaves it. Every night, in secret, she unpicks it. It is never finished. Then she sets a contest.

String Odysseus's great bow and shoot an arrow clean through a line of axe-heads, twelve of them in the poem, stood in a row. Every suitor tries. Every suitor fails. The ragged beggar picks it up and strings it like it

is nothing. Then he turns the bow on the room, and with his son beside him, kills every last suitor in the hall. The moment the whole poem has been building toward. There is one final test.

Penelope still is not sure the stranger is truly her husband. So she casually orders a servant to move their marriage bed.

And Odysseus snaps, because he built that bed himself, and one post of it is a living olive tree, still rooted in the ground.

The bed cannot be moved. Only the real husband would know that. That is how she knows him. So that is the fairy tale.

Now the digging. Because starting in the eighteen seventys, people went looking for the real Troy. And what they found is stranger than the story.

Here is the first shock. There really is a Troy.

A hill in northwest Turkey called Hisarlik, guarding the sea route between the Aegean and the Black Sea. And it is not one city.

It is nine, built one on top of another over thousands of years.

The man who found it was a wealthy German businessman named Heinrich Schliemann. In eighteen seventy-three, he announced he had found Homer's Troy. And he pulled a hoard of gold out of the ground and named it Priam's Treasure.

There is just one problem, and here is the part almost nobody tells you. That gold is real. But it is about a thousand years too old.

It belongs to a version of the city, called Troy Two, from around twenty-two hundred BC, long before any possible Trojan War.

Schliemann was so hungry to reach it that he cut a giant trench straight down through the mound, and destroyed the very layer that might actually have been Homer's Troy. So which layer is the real one? The best guess is one archaeologists

call Troy Seven-A. And it ended in violence. Arrowheads buried in the walls. Houses burned black. Bodies left unburied. Something attacked this city and destroyed

it. When exactly? We do not know for sure, somewhere between about twelve fifty and eleven eighty BC, depending on which expert

you ask. And later digs uncovered a whole lower town outside the walls. This was no village. It was a wealthy city on a key trade route, big enough

to be worth fighting over. But here is the honest part. Finding a burned city is not the same as proving the war. Many scholars think some real conflict lies behind the legend, probably a fight over that

trade route. But a ten-year siege, the wooden horse, Helen, those we simply cannot confirm. We cannot even be certain these particular ruins are the

same Troy that Homer had in mind. So if the war is uncertain, what part

is solid? The world. The heroes in the poem come from a real civilization, the Mycenaeans. Bronze Age Greeks, from around seventeen hundred to

twelve hundred BC. They built fortified palaces behind massive stone walls we still call Cyclopean, and buried their kings in great beehive tombs

of stone. And they could write. They kept palace records in a script we call Linear B. For a long time, nobody could read it.

Then in nineteen fifty-two, a man named Michael Ventris cracked it. And the language underneath turned out to be an early form of

Greek. Homer's heroes really were Greeks.

Not a fantasy people. A real one. One of these palaces belonged to a king named Nestor, who is also a character in the poem.

It burned down around eleven eighty BC, and the fire baked its clay record-tablets rock hard, accidentally preserving the palace's accounts from its very last

year. Because that whole world was ending. Around twelve hundred BC, the entire eastern Mediterranean fell apart at once. Palace after palace

burned. Empires collapsed. Raiders roamed the sea. Nobody is sure why, whether drought, earthquakes, invasion, or a whole trade

network unravelling at once. Afterward, Greece slid into a dark age, and forgot how to write for centuries. So now we have a real problem.

Sit with it for a second. The poem describes a world that ended around twelve hundred BC. But Homer, the poet we credit with it, probably lived around eight hundred BC. That is four to five hundred years later. And in between sits a dark

age with no writing at all. So how does a story survive four centuries with nobody writing it down? The answer is the strangest thing in all of this.

It survived because people sang it. For all those centuries, the Odyssey was not a book. It was a song. Performed live, from memory, by traveling singers, over and over, generation after generation.

Two scholars, Milman Parry and Albert Lord, worked out how. They studied living singers who still did exactly this, and found the trick.

The singers built the poem out of ready-made phrases that fit the rhythm. The wine-dark sea. Rosy-fingered dawn. Little repeated blocks that make an enormous poem possible to hold inside one human head.

And Homer himself? We are not even sure he was one person. He might have been. Or the name might just be a label we stuck on that whole centuries-long chain of singers. Nobody knows. Now here is the payoff, the

thing that proves the memory machine truly worked. In his other poem, the Iliad, Homer describes a very specific helmet.

Made from rows of boar's tusks, roughly forty or fifty wild boars' worth, stitched onto a cap. And here is the impossible part.

Nobody in Homer's own lifetime wore a helmet like that. It had been out of use for centuries. He was describing an object he had, by

every right, never seen. Then archaeologists started opening Mycenaean graves. And there it was. Exactly that helmet.

Rows of boar's tusks, just as described. A sung poem had carried the memory of a real object across five hundred years, accurately, with

nobody writing a single word of it down. So, which parts were real?

Here is where even the experts land. The city of Troy, found. The world of the Mycenaeans, real, and Greek. The boar's-tusk helmet, a genuine memory smuggled out of the Bronze Age by

a song. But the war itself? The wooden horse? Helen? Odysseus himself? The honest answer, from the people who have studied this their whole lives, is that nobody knows for certain.

There is no evidence any Odysseus ever lived. The hero is legend, even where his world was real. And here is the strangest part.

Remember those words I said you had used today, without noticing? That is this poem, still living quietly inside your language.

Caught between two dangers? You are caught between Scylla and Charybdis. A long, hard journey? That is an odyssey.

A hidden trap that arrives looking like a gift? A Trojan horse, now even the name for a kind of computer virus. A song nearly three thousand years

old, still hiding inside the words in your mouth.

So maybe that is the real magic of it. The Odyssey is not a documentary, and it is not a fairy tale. It is a memory. Half real, half invented.

Passed mouth to mouth for so long that the true parts and the dreamed parts fused into one story we can no longer fully pull apart.

We started by calling it make-believe. Then we dug, and the make-believe kept coming true, one impossible detail at a time. A real city. A real people. A real helmet, remembered by

a song. And still, nobody can tell you for certain how much of the rest ever happened. But maybe that is the point. Maybe a story lasts three thousand years precisely because it never lets us finish arguing about what was real.

We are still watching it on the biggest screens we can build, and still asking. A story that simply refuses to stop being alive.

So here is what we do here. We take the stories you think you know, the legends and the empires, and we go digging for what is actually real underneath. Subscribe, and we will keep digging together.

---

## The Ottoman Empire Killed Rome — Then Killed Itself

URL: https://doodlehistory.com/episodes/ottoman/
Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Vq8s0bpIaT4
Published: 2026-07-23 · Length: 13 min

The Ottoman Empire began as a tiny band of frontier raiders and grew into the empire that finished the Roman story: in 1453 a twenty-one-year-old sultan broke the thousand-year walls of Constantinople and ended the last Roman Empire. For more than six centuries the Ottomans ruled across three continents, then dismantled themselves in barely twelve years. This is the complete rise and fall of the Ottoman Empire.

The full history of the Ottoman Empire explained: how Osman founded the empire around the year 1300, how Mehmed the Conqueror took Constantinople in 1453, how the devshirme levy and the janissaries built the first professional army in Europe since Rome, the golden age of Suleiman the Magnificent, the turning point at the gates of Vienna in 1683, why the Ottomans became the 'sick man of Europe,' and how the empire finally collapsed through the Balkan Wars and the First World War. A Doodle History documentary on how the Ottoman Empire rose, ruled, and fell. Six centuries of military history: the siege of Constantinople in 1453, the janissary armies, and the battles of Mohács, Lepanto and Vienna that shaped Europe and the Middle East.

Transcript:

This is the empire that killed Rome. Not the Rome of four hundred seventy-six that fell to barbarians. But the last Roman Empire, the eastern half

that survived another thousand years behind unbreakable walls.

In the spring of fourteen fifty-three, the Ottomans finally broke those walls and ended the Roman story for good. And then, six centuries

later, this same empire did something no army ever managed to do to it. It destroyed itself, in barely twelve years.

Because the thing that made it unstoppable was the same thing that doomed it.

The Ottomans were a machine built for one purpose, conquest, and a machine built only to expand cannot survive the day it stops moving.

So let's start the countdown. It begins with almost nothing.

Around the year thirteen hundred, on the shrinking edge of a dying Byzantium, there is a frontier warlord named Osman. He leads a small band of Turkish raiders in the hills of northwestern Anatolia. He has a legend, not a kingdom.

The story goes that he dreamed of a tree growing from his body to shade the whole world. By some accounts he was founded around the year twelve ninety-nine, but that date is really a later legend, not a document.

What we can point to is a battle, around thirteen oh one, where Osman's raiders crush a Byzantine army. That is the moment the raiders become conquerors.

His son Orhan takes the city of Bursa in the thirteen twentys and gives the state its first capital. And then they do something no one expects.

They cross the water into Europe. In thirteen fifty-four they seize Gallipoli, a permanent foothold on the European shore. They plant a capital at Edirne in Thrace. They are standing on European soil a full hundred years before

they take Constantinople. But how does a band of frontier raiders build an army that terrifies all of Christendom? Here is the answer, and it is one of the strangest ideas in the history of war.

Every so often, Ottoman officials ride into a Christian village in the Balkans. They take the boys. Boys from Albania, from Bosnia, from Serbia, from Greece, mostly in their teens.

The boys are marched away from their mothers, converted to Islam, and trained for the sultan's service. And here is the part nobody tells you.

The most feared soldiers in Europe were kidnapped Christian children. They became the janissaries, an elite standing infantry, the first professional army

the continent had seen since Rome. By law, these men were technically the sultan's slaves. And yet a slave-boy taken from a village could rise all the way to grand vizier and run the empire. The Ottoman war machine was

built out of its own captured children. With that machine, the sultans drive deeper into Europe.

In thirteen eighty-nine, on a plain called Kosovo, the Ottoman army meets a Serbian-led alliance for the fate of the Balkans. The battle is savage, and by the end the Serbian resistance is broken. But in the middle of that field, Sultan

Murad the First is killed. The victorious sultan lies dead on

the ground he has just won. Even so, the outcome holds.

After Kosovo, the Ottomans are the masters of southeastern Europe. The countdown ticks on. But the countdown almost ends before it truly begins.

In fourteen oh two, a new conqueror comes storming out of the east. His name is Timur, and he is a whirlwind. At the Battle of Ankara

he shatters Sultan Bayezid the First and takes him prisoner. Think about that. The only Ottoman sultan ever captured by an enemy.

Bayezid dies in captivity the next year. And the empire tears itself apart, as his sons fight an eleven-year civil war for the throne.

For over a decade, the Ottomans nearly cease to exist.

A century before their peak, they stare into the grave.

Then a son named Mehmed the First stitches the empire back together and is remembered as its second founder. The countdown resets. And it points straight at those thousand-year-old walls.

twenty-nine May fourteen fifty-three. The sultan is Mehmed the Second, and he is twenty-one years old. In front of him stand the Theodosian Walls, finished a thousand years before, never broken. Behind those walls,

the defenders are desperately few. By most estimates, only a few thousand men, many of them Italian allies from Genoa and Venice. Outside the walls waits an Ottoman army of tens of thousands.

But numbers were never what cracked Constantinople. The real weapon was a machine. A cannon-founder named Orban, a Hungarian, had first offered his services to

the Byzantines. They could not pay him. So he built his monster

for the sultan instead. Accounts describe a bronze bombard on the order of eight or nine meters long, hurling stone balls weighing several hundred kilograms. It was so vast it could only be fired a handful of times

a day, needing hours to cool. But around it roared dozens of smaller guns, firing again and again. Together they battered the walls faster than the defenders could rebuild them. For roughly seven or eight weeks

the pounding went on. And then the walls that had stood for a thousand years came down. The last Roman emperor, Constantine the Eleventh, died

fighting in the final assault. By tradition he threw off his imperial robes to die as an ordinary soldier, and his body was never certainly found. The eleven-hundred-year Roman story ended in that morning.

And a new capital was born. Constantinople was now the seat of the Ottoman sultans. For a century after, the empire only rises.

Under Selim the First, nicknamed the Grim, it explodes outward. First he turns east, against the rival Safavid Persians.

In fifteen fourteen, at a place called Chaldiran, his guns tear the Persian cavalry apart. The victory secures his eastern frontier and

frees his hand to strike south. And then, in barely a year, from fifteen sixteen to fifteen seventeen, he swallows the Mamluk Sultanate whole. Syria, Egypt, and the holy land of the Hejaz

all fall under Ottoman rule. And with them come Mecca and Medina, the holiest cities of Islam. The sultan now claims the caliphate itself,

leadership of the Sunni Muslim world. Then comes the golden age. Under Suleiman, the man Europe called the Magnificent, the empire reaches its peak. His own people called him Kanuni, the

Lawgiver, for the code of law he built. He ruled at least around twenty-five million subjects across three continents. At its height the empire sprawled over five million square kilometers.

And Suleiman wastes no time turning that power on Europe. In fifteen twenty-one he storms Belgrade, the great fortress guarding the road

into central Europe. The next year, in fifteen twenty-two, he takes the island of Rhodes and clears its Christian knights from the eastern

sea. Belgrade opens the road to Hungary, and beyond Hungary lies Vienna. In fifteen twenty-six, at Mohács, Suleiman destroys the entire army of the King of Hungary in about two hours.

The young king drowns fleeing the field, and the medieval Kingdom of Hungary simply ceases to exist. Three years later, Suleiman is at the gates of Vienna

itself. This is the high-water mark, the deepest the Ottoman tide will ever reach into western Europe. But behind all that glory, the palace

hid something dark. The Ottomans had a law of fratricide. When a new sultan took the throne, he was permitted to have his own brothers

killed, to prevent civil war. For the good order of the world, the law said.

In fifteen ninety-five, a sultan named Mehmed the Third took the throne and had nineteen of his brothers and half-brothers strangled with silk bowstrings. By some accounts the youngest was a boy of about eleven.

Later, they stopped killing the princes and started caging them instead. Rival heirs were locked for life inside the palace harem, cut off from the world. So some sultans reached the throne after spending decades sealed

away in a gilded cage, knowing nothing. An empire at its peak was quietly

poisoning its own future rulers. Now the countdown turns the other way.

In fifteen seventy-one, a Christian fleet meets the Ottoman navy at Lepanto and destroys it. It is the first great naval defeat, a shock across

the empire. But it does not stick. The Ottomans rebuild their whole fleet within about a year and keep Cyprus anyway.

The real turning point comes in the autumn of sixteen eighty-three. Once again an Ottoman army is at the gates of Vienna. The grand vizier Kara Mustafa is certain the city

will fall. And then, over the hills, comes a relief army led by the King of Poland, Jan Sobieski.

Down the slope charges his cavalry, the winged hussars, in what is often called the largest cavalry charge in history. The Ottoman army is shattered. The siege breaks.

And this time the tide does not just pause. It reverses, for good. By the treaty that follows in sixteen

ninety-nine, the Ottomans hand Hungary to the Habsburgs.

For the first time in their history, they sign as a defeated, shrinking power.

The terror of Europe has begun to retreat. And the retreat becomes a long, grinding

bleed. By the eighteen hundreds, the empire has a cruel new nickname.

The label is usually traced to the Russian tsar, Nicholas the First, who in eighteen fifty-three called the empire a sick man. The terror of Europe was now the sick man of Europe.

Province after province breaks away. Greece wins its independence, an early piece torn from the map. The empire tries desperately to save

itself by changing. In eighteen twenty-six the sultan turns

on his own janissaries. When the old corps mutinies against reform, thousands of them are killed in a single violent purge. The elite that had conquered Constantinople

is wiped out to make room for a modern army. Then come the Tanzimat reforms, a genuine attempt to remake the empire along European lines, with new laws and equality

for all subjects. But the reforms come too late, and cost too much. By eighteen seventy-five the empire is bankrupt, defaulting

on its enormous European loans. And soon a European-run debt administration is seizing Ottoman revenues to pay foreign creditors.

The empire that once dictated terms to Europe now can't even control its

own money. By now a new generation has stopped waiting on the sultan. In nineteen oh eight, a movement of young officers, the Young Turks, forces the old ruler to restore the constitution he had suspended.

The next year they depose him outright, and Sultan Abdul Hamid the Second is stripped of his throne. The sultan now sits under men who no

longer truly obey him. An empire trying to reform itself has instead started deposing its own rulers. And then, in a single generation,

the whole thing collapses. In nineteen twelve, a coalition of small Balkan states goes to war with the Ottomans.

In a matter of weeks, they drive the empire out of almost all its remaining European land. Provinces held for over five hundred years are gone almost

overnight. Two years later, the empire makes one last fatal gamble. It enters the First World War on the side of Germany.

At Gallipoli in nineteen fifteen, Ottoman forces repel a massive Allied assault, and a young officer named Mustafa Kemal wins fame in the defense.

But the war is tearing the empire apart from the inside.

Encouraged by Britain, the Arabs rise in revolt and its Middle Eastern provinces slip away. And in the same terrible years, the Ottoman

government carries out the Armenian genocide, the mass deportation

and killing of its Armenian population, with deaths estimated on

the order of a million or more. By the autumn of nineteen eighteen, it is

over. The Ottomans sign an armistice and the Allies move to carve up what remains. But out of the wreckage rises Mustafa Kemal.

He fights a war of independence against the partition and wins a Turkish state from

the ruins. And then comes the final image of a six-hundred-year empire.

On one November nineteen twenty-two, the assembly in Ankara abolishes the sultanate. Days later, the last sultan, Mehmed the Sixth,

quietly slips out of Constantinople, into exile, aboard a British warship.

Two years after that, the caliphate itself is abolished and the last caliph sent

away. The dynasty that Osman began around the year thirteen hundred was

finished. And the Republic of Turkey rose in its place.

So think about the whole arc. Rome fell, and stayed fallen.

The eastern half survived a thousand years more, until the Ottomans ended it in one morning in fourteen fifty-three. An empire that had literally

outlasted and destroyed Rome then took itself apart in barely twelve years. The countdown that started with a single warlord's dream ended

with a lone sultan sailing away on someone else's ship.

It was never really beaten by Europe. It was beaten by the day it stopped moving.

If you want to see how the next great empire rose, a glittering civilization that built a city on a lake and then fell to a few hundred strangers in barely two years, subscribe, because next time on Greatest Empires, we

tell the story of the Aztecs.

## Imperial China Died a Dozen Times and Refused to Stay Dead

URL: https://doodlehistory.com/episodes/imperial-china/
Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ZFIcwb2HH4g
Published: 2026-07-16 · Length: 12 min

China is not the oldest unbroken empire on Earth — it is something far stranger. This is the rise and fall of imperial China: an empire that violently collapsed and was reborn a dozen times across two thousand years, from the First Emperor Qin Shi Huang to the last emperor Puyi, all driven by the Mandate of Heaven.

Imperial China explained — the full sweep of the Chinese dynasties, from Qin Shi Huang and the Terracotta Army through the Han, Tang, Song, Ming and Qing, the Mandate of Heaven, and the dynastic cycle that let China collapse and be reborn a dozen times across two thousand years. Two thousand years of Chinese civilization and military history: dynasties, rebellions and invasions — and the imperial system that kept resurrecting after every collapse.

Transcript:

You've heard that China is the oldest empire on earth. One unbroken line. One eternal civilization that never fell. That story is a myth. The truth is the opposite, and it's far more astonishing. This empire didn't survive for two thousand years.

It died. Over and over. A dozen times it collapsed in fire and rebellion, and a dozen times it clawed its way back from the grave.

And here's the part I can't get past. Most things that break, stay broken. This empire did the opposite. It turned dying, and clawing its way back, into its whole way of being. So how do you outlast Rome

and Egypt by dying again and again? The answer is a single, ruthless idea. The Chinese called it the Mandate of Heaven. Picture a contract written by the sky itself. Heaven blesses a just ruler. The moment that ruler turns cruel, Heaven yanks the blessing away.

And here's the deadly twist. If a rebel wins, that victory was the proof. Heaven had already switched sides. So every successful uprising became holy. Every new emperor was Heaven's new choice.

That one idea is the engine that drove the rise and fall of imperial China,

again and again, for over two thousand years. It begins with one of

the most terrifying men who ever lived. Around two hundred twenty-one BC,

after centuries of warring states tearing each other apart, a single king conquered them all. His name was Ying Zheng. And he wanted a title no

one had ever held. So he invented one. Emperor. He called himself Qin Shi Huang, the First Emperor.

And the word he coined for "emperor" would be spoken by Chinese rulers for the next two

thousand years. But unifying the map wasn't enough for him.

He unified everything. He forced every region to use the same written script. The same round coins. The same weights and measures. He even standardized the width of cart axles, so every wagon fit every road

in the empire. Imagine erasing every local difference in a land that vast, by decree. And he was brutal about it. The Qin ruled by a cold philosophy called Legalism.

Harsh laws. Collective punishment. Total control. By the traditional account, the regime burned books it disliked and buried hundreds

of scholars alive. Knowledge itself was a threat to the state.

To wall out the horsemen of the northern steppe, he linked older frontier walls

into a first Great Wall. And for his own death, he built an army. Deep near modern Xi'an, archaeologists later uncovered the Terracotta Army. By some accounts, several thousand life-size clay soldiers, each with its own face, standing guard over an emperor's tomb for eternity.

Ancient texts claim hundreds of thousands of laborers built it.

So here's the question. A man this powerful. An empire this total. How long do you think it lasted? Roughly fifteen years. That's it. The First Emperor died, and the whole machine shattered in revolt

almost immediately. The very harshness that built the empire is what destroyed

it. By the logic of the Mandate, Heaven had spoken.

And out of the wreckage rose a commoner named Liu Bang, who won the war

and founded a dynasty that would become legend. The Han. The Han is China's first golden age.

It glowed so brightly that, even today, the majority ethnic group in China calls itself the Han people, named after this very dynasty.

Under Emperor Wu, a thinker named Confucius became the state's official guide. His ideas about order, family, and duty would shape Chinese government for two thousand years. And the Han reached outward. A diplomat named Zhang Qian

rode west into the unknown, and his journeys cracked open the Silk Road.

Suddenly Chinese silk was flowing all the way to Rome, and Rome's gold was flowing back. Two great empires, on opposite ends of the earth, trading without ever truly meeting. Then came an invention that changed the human mind itself. A court official named Cai Lun

is credited with refining cheap paper, made from bark, hemp, and old rags. Now ideas could be written down for almost nothing, and spread. Paper would eventually travel the whole world. But the Han's greatest creation was

quieter. They began choosing officials by merit. Recommend a man, then test him. It was the seed of an idea that would outlive every dynasty to come. And then, after four centuries,

even the mighty Han rotted, collapsed, and fell.

China shattered into pieces for roughly four hundred years.

Now, here's the part nobody tells you about Chinese history. We talk about it as one smooth story. It wasn't.

Between the golden ages were long, bloody centuries of chaos, where the empire

simply did not exist. China spent enormous stretches of its life

broken into warring kingdoms. The miracle isn't that it lasted.

The miracle is that it kept choosing to reassemble itself, every single time,

from the rubble. And reassemble it did. A dynasty called the Sui stitched the country back together. They dug the Grand Canal, a colossal artificial river linking the Yellow River in the north to the Yangtze in the south. It tied the rice-rich south to the political

north, and it was built by armies of conscripted laborers at a horrifying

human cost. That overreach, plus disastrous wars, burned

the Sui out in just a few decades. But the canal remained.

And on that foundation rose one of the most dazzling empires in human history. The Tang. The Tang was cosmopolitan, confident, and open to the world.

Its capital, Chang'an, swelled to roughly a million people inside the walls, making it likely the largest city on earth. Walk its streets and

you'd pass merchants from Persia, envoys from Korea and Japan, and temples of half a dozen faiths standing side by side. It was the great age of Chinese poetry, with masters like Li Bai and Du

Fu. And the Tang did something no other dynasty ever did.

For fifteen years, it was ruled by a woman who held the actual title of emperor. Her name was Wu Zetian. She seized supreme power, founded her own dynasty, and ruled in her own right. The only female emperor in the entire history of China.

Then a devastating rebellion gutted the Tang, regional warlords carved

up its power, and by nine hundred seven this golden age, too, was gone. But watch what China loses and what it keeps. Dynasties die. The civilization underneath them does not. Because the next empire

would be the most inventive of them all. The Song dynasty was a medieval explosion of technology and money. Three of China's four great inventions matured or spread here. Gunpowder, with its first written formulas appearing around the year ten forty-four. The magnetic compass, which let ships

find their way across open sea. And printing, including movable type, centuries before Europe. The Song even issued the world's first government paper money, real banknotes, while Europe was still counting coins. This was a society centuries ahead of the rest of the world.

And then, from the grasslands of the north, came a storm it could not survive.

If those horsemen sound familiar, they should. Because the conquerors were

the same Mongols we followed last time. The grandson of Genghis Khan, a warlord named Kublai Khan, set his eyes on all of China. He proclaimed a new dynasty, the Yuan, and by twelve seventy-nine he had crushed the last Song resistance. And here is the moment that broke a thousand

years of pride. For the first time ever, the whole of China was ruled by a foreign people. Outsiders sat on the dragon throne.

The conquering Mongols ruled from a city they called Khanbaliq. Today we call that city Beijing. And it was here, by his own account,

that a Venetian traveler named Marco Polo reportedly visited the great Khan's court. But the Mandate is a cruel master, even to conquerors. Famine, plague, and rebellion broke Mongol rule in under a century.

And the man who drove them out was as low-born as it gets. A starving peasant who became a wandering monk, then a rebel general, then

an emperor. His name was Zhu Yuanzhang, and his Ming dynasty was

a proud restoration of native Han rule. The Ming built the China of postcards. The Forbidden City in Beijing, an entire palace city raised by hundreds

of thousands of workers, became the emperor's home for the rest of the empire's

life. And the Great Wall you picture in your mind, that magnificent stone serpent across the mountains, is mostly a Ming creation. The wall they rebuilt in brick is far younger than the First Emperor's original.

And for one brief, breathtaking window, the Ming looked outward. A Muslim admiral named Zheng He commanded enormous treasure fleets that sailed across the Indian Ocean. By some accounts these were among the largest wooden ships ever built. They reached Southeast Asia, India,

Arabia, and the coast of East Africa, decades before Columbus crossed the Atlantic. China was poised to discover the world.

And then it simply stopped. The voyages were abruptly cancelled.

The great fleets were left to rot. The Ming turned its back on

the sea and looked inward, behind its new walls.

It's one of history's great what-ifs. What if China had kept sailing?

Instead, the Mandate turned one final time.

In sixteen forty-four, rebels stormed Beijing, the last Ming emperor died,

and a new northern people, the Manchus, swept in to seize the throne. Their dynasty was the Qing. And once again, a foreign minority ruled the vast Chinese majority. At first, the Qing soared. Under a run of brilliant emperors, the empire reached its greatest size ever, and its

population would eventually pass four hundred million people. It was the largest empire China had ever been. The peak before the long fall. Because this time, the danger didn't come from the steppe. It came by sea, from an industrial Europe the old empire could not comprehend.

Britain wanted to sell opium into China. When the Qing said no, Britain went to war, and won easily. The First Opium War forced a humiliating treaty on China. Then a second war forced more. The proud empire was being carved up by foreigners, and there was little it could do. The Chinese remember this era by a

bitter name. The century of humiliation. And from within, it bled

too. A vast civil war called the Taiping Rebellion tore through the country, killing, by some estimates, twenty to thirty million people,

one of the deadliest conflicts in all of human history.

The empire was dying its final death. In nineteen oh five, the Qing abolished

the imperial exam system, that meritocratic road to power, after roughly thirteen hundred years.

The oldest institution of Chinese government was gone.

And the end, when it came, was strangely quiet.

The last emperor of China was a little boy named Puyi. He took the throne at under three years old, a toddler in a robe in the Forbidden City,

ruling over a fifth of humanity. In nineteen twelve, a revolution swept

the dynasty away, and on a cold February day, the child-emperor abdicated. With one signature, over two thousand years of imperial rule came to an end.

Puyi would live on as a puppet, a prisoner, and finally as an ordinary citizen who died, decades later, working in a garden. So look at the whole impossible

arc. Qin to Han. Tang to Song. Yuan to Ming to Qing. Each dynasty rose, glittered, rotted, and fell, and each time the same civilization rebuilt itself on the ashes.

And now you can see why the myth gets it so wrong, and why the truth is so

much greater. China was never one unbroken, eternal empire. It was something stranger. It was an empire that kept dying and refused to stay dead. Think back. Rome fell once, and stayed fallen forever.

Egypt was finally swallowed whole by outsiders and never ruled itself again.

But China, broken a dozen times, conquered, humiliated, shattered, always pulled itself back into the same civilization. And along the way it handed the world paper, printing, gunpowder, and the compass, the very tools that would remake everyone else.

And here's what stays with me. We are taught that surviving means never falling. China spent two thousand years proving the exact opposite. Maybe that's the real secret of imperial China. It wasn't built to never fall. It was built to be reborn. We've now watched three of history's giants.

The one that fell once. The one that was swallowed. And the one that simply would not die.

Next time, we follow another empire that thought it would last forever. If you want to know which one, stay with me.

---

## Genghis Khan Started as a Boy Left for Dead

URL: https://doodlehistory.com/episodes/mongol-empire/
Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=lbQGg1PqfAo
Published: 2026-07-09 · Length: 11 min

A starving orphan his own clan abandoned to die on the freezing steppe became the founder of the largest land empire in history. This is the true story of Genghis Khan and the rise of the Mongol Empire — and the one idea that let him outgrow the world that threw him away.

The Mongol Empire explained — how Genghis Khan rose from an abandoned, enslaved boy to forge the largest contiguous land empire in history, sweeping from China to the gates of Europe, and how the empire fractured almost as fast as it was built. A military history of the medieval world: Genghis Khan's armies, the sieges and conquests that built the largest contiguous land empire in history, and the trade routes it connected.

Chapters:
  0:00 Not a Barbarian
  0:46 Abandoned on the Steppe
  2:19 Captive and Escape
  3:08 The Climb: Allies and Betrayal
  4:53 1206: Genghis Khan
  5:22 The War Machine
  7:31 Conquest and Catastrophe
  9:09 Death and the Empire That Outgrew Him

  - Genghis Khan — Encyclopaedia Britannica (https://www.britannica.com/biography/Genghis-Khan)

Transcript:

We call him a world-conquering tyrant.

But here's what the legend leaves out. His story starts with him losing. A chief's son, suddenly fatherless.

Abandoned by his own clan, foraging for roots and crunching wild nuts just to survive another day. The most powerful man of his age

began as the boy everyone had already written off.

Forget everything the name Genghis Khan makes you picture. This is where it actually starts. And my take is this.

He didn't conquer the world by being the cruelest man in it. He won with one idea the great, proud kingdoms were too arrogant to copy. He trusted people for what they could do, not who they were born to be.

So how does a child left for dead end up ruling more land than anyone in history?

Let's go back to where it falls apart. His name was Temüjin.

By most accounts he was born around the year eleven sixty-two, near a cold

river on the Mongolian steppe. His father, Yesügei, was a chief of the proud Borjigin clan. For a few short years, Temüjin was somebody. A chief's son. A boy with a future.

Then, when he was about nine, his father rode out and shared a meal with strangers. The strangers were Tatars, old enemies who recognized his

face. By the cruel logic of steppe hospitality, they could not refuse him food, so they slipped poison into it instead.

Yesügei made it home, sickened, and died.

And the moment he was gone, the clan made a cold calculation. A widow and her small children could not lead them. So why follow them at

all? The rival Tayichiud family packed the camp and rode off, taking everything, leaving Temüjin's mother and her babies alone on the open

grass. Picture it. A whole tribe turning their backs. A future emperor watching the dust trail vanish over the hill.

This is the bottom. This is as low as it gets. The family survived by digging roots out of the dirt and crunching wild nuts. They hunted tiny animals and pulled fish from the river just to eat another day.

The Secret History of the Mongols even records a darker moment from these years.

In a bitter fight over food, Temüjin and his brother Qasar killed their own older half-brother, Bekter. The official chronicles later

left that part out. It was not the story of a hero.

But here's the thing about Temüjin. Surviving was not the same as being safe. The old rival clan still saw him as a threat, even now, even as a half-starved boy. So they hunted him down and captured him.

By tradition, they locked his neck in a heavy wooden collar, a wooden yoke he could barely lift. He was paraded as a prisoner, helpless, a captive of the very people who had abandoned him. And this is the moment the whole

future hangs by a thread. During a feast, with his guards drunk and careless, a sympathetic captor named Sorkan-Shira looked the other way. He hid the boy at enormous risk to his own life. Temüjin slipped

his collar and ran into the dark. Stop and sit with that.

The man who would conquer half the world once escaped a feast wearing a wooden yoke around his neck. Now watch the climb begin.

A boy with nothing has only one weapon left. Loyalty. The ability to make people believe in him. So Temüjin started collecting allies.

He swore the anda bond, the blood-brother oath, with a charismatic young

chief named Jamukha. He went to his late father's old friend, the powerful Toghrul of the Kerait, and won his protection. Then came the test.

He married a young woman named Börte. And almost at once, a rival tribe, the Merkits, swept in and kidnapped her.

The old Temüjin would have lost her forever. The new one called in his favors.

With Toghrul's warriors and Jamukha at his side, he rode down the raiders and tore his wife back out of their hands. That rescue was the proof.

People started to see that this outcast could lead. But power on the steppe

was a snake pit, and friends became rivals fast.

Temüjin and his blood-brother Jamukha drifted apart, then turned on each other for control of the tribes. And his old patron Toghrul?

In twelve oh three the Kerait khan turned against him too. After a desperate reversal of fortune, Temüjin surrounded the Keraits and shattered them. Toghrul fled and was killed. One year later, in

twelve oh four, he crushed the last great holdout, the Naimans. His old anda Jamukha was finally handed over to him, and executed.

And here's the part nobody tells you about the man we call a barbarian.

When he won, he did not simply slaughter the talented men of the tribes he beat. He hired them. There was a warrior named Jebe who, in battle,

had shot Genghis Khan's own horse out from under him. Most warlords would have him killed slowly. Genghis Khan made him a general.

Loyalty and skill, he decided, were worth more than revenge. That idea would build an empire. By now the abandoned orphan was

the most powerful man on the steppe. So in twelve oh six, the tribes gathered for a great assembly, a kurultai, at the source of the

Onon River. There, they proclaimed Temüjin the supreme ruler of them all, with a new name. Genghis Khan. A title usually taken

to mean something like universal, or oceanic, ruler.

The boy left to die in the grass was now the lord of every tent on the steppe. The flip was complete. But it was only the beginning.

Because now the question changes. How did a few scattered herding tribes conquer the most powerful kingdoms on Earth? The answer is that Genghis Khan did

not just build an army. He built a machine. He tore up the old tribal loyalties and reorganized everyone by the number ten.

Squads of ten, companies of a hundred, regiments of a thousand, and divisions of ten thousand called tumen. He deliberately mixed

men from different tribes together, so their only loyalty was to him.

Then he did something almost no king of his age would dare. He promoted by talent, not birth. His greatest general, Subutai,

was the son of a blacksmith. His other commanders were sons of carpenters, shepherds, and herdsmen. Low men who became

legends. The weapon itself was the Mongol horse-archer. A rider on a tough little pony, firing a powerful composite bow at full gallop.

And here was the trick. Each man led a string of spare horses. When one mount tired, he leapt to a fresh one and kept moving, covering distances

that left enemies stunned. Their favorite tactic was the feigned

retreat. They would pretend to flee in panic. The enemy would chase, break their lines, and ride straight into a trap of arrows.

But a man can't just conquer. He has to rule. So Genghis Khan built the bones of a state. He had a written script created

for the Mongol language, borrowing the Uighur alphabet. He issued a body of law tied to his name, known as the Yassa.

He decreed religious freedom, letting the great faiths be practiced across

his lands, which was rare for the age. His armies were weak at attacking walled cities, so he simply absorbed the engineers who could. Chinese and Persian siege specialists, with their catapults, became Mongol tools.

And stitching it all together was the Yam, a relay of way-stations roughly a day's ride apart. Fresh horses waited at each one, so a single message

could fly across thousands of miles of empire. By the late thirteenth century, sources describe something on the order of ten thousand of these stations.

A machine built for speed, for loyalty, and for terror.

Now he aimed it outward. First he turned on the Western Xia kingdom and forced it to bow around twelve oh nine and twelve ten.

Then in twelve eleven he invaded the mighty Jin dynasty of northern China. By twelve fifteen, his riders had sacked its great capital, Zhongdu, near modern Beijing. The orphan was now humbling emperors.

But the war that defined his reputation was one he didn't even start.

To the west lay the wealthy Khwarazmian Empire, and Genghis Khan wanted trade, not blood. So he sent a huge, peaceful merchant caravan to do business.

At the border city of Otrar, the local governor, Inalchuq, seized the whole caravan and executed the traders as spies. Genghis Khan, furious

but restrained, sent envoys to demand justice. Now, to the Mongols,

an envoy was sacred. To harm a messenger was an unforgivable crime. So when the Shah killed one of those envoys and shamed the others, he wasn't insulting a man. He was signing a death warrant for his entire

empire. What came next was one of history's most terrible storms. From twelve nineteen onward, the Mongols poured into

Khwarazmia, and the great cities began to fall. Otrar, Bukhara, Samarkand, Urgench, Nishapur, Merv. One by one, the jewels of the region. Medieval chroniclers describe

massacres so vast they claimed over a million dead in a single city. Though modern historians believe those numbers are greatly inflated, since the cities could never have held that many people. What's clear is that the destruction

was real, and it was meant to make the whole world afraid to resist.

And then, at the height of it all, the conqueror's own story ran out. In twelve twenty-seven, while crushing a final rebellion by the Western Xia, Genghis Khan died, aged around sixty-five. By some accounts he fell from his

horse. By others he sickened. The true cause is simply unknown.

His followers buried him in secret, and where they laid him is a mystery to this day. Legend says his escort killed anyone who saw the grave, so it could never be found. But here is the strangest

twist of all. The largest empire ever, the one his name is forever tied to, did not exist when he died. After a pause, his

third son Ögedei was raised up as Great Khan in twelve twenty-nine. And it was his sons and grandsons who pushed the borders to their greatest reach.

His grandson Kublai conquered all of China. His grandson Batu drove the Golden Horde deep into Eastern Europe.

At its peak, the empire spread across roughly twenty-four million square kilometers. The largest single connected stretch of land any empire has ever ruled, governing on the order of a hundred million people. And under that vast Mongol peace,

something unexpected bloomed. The same roads built for war now made

the Silk Road safe. Goods, ideas, and travelers like Marco Polo flowed clear across a single, connected Eurasia.

Merchants used paper money backed by silk and silver, which left European visitors astonished. Though there was a darker legacy too.

Those same open roads are often credited, in a debate that still runs today, with helping carry the Black Death west into Europe in the thirteen fortys.

For better and for worse, the orphan on the grass had rewired the world.

And that's the gap I keep coming back to. A boy whose own clan left him to die, with a wooden collar around his neck and roots in his hand.

He didn't just survive them. He outgrew the entire world that abandoned him.

And he did it the way nobody expected. The empires with the biggest walls and the oldest bloodlines lost to the one ruler humble enough to hand a blacksmith's

son command of his armies. If a half-starved outcast on the empty steppe could become the largest empire in history, what does that

say about every person we've ever written off? Stick around, because the next chapter is another empire, another impossible story, built by someone nobody saw coming.

## Ancient Egypt: 3,000 Years Nothing Could Conquer

URL: https://doodlehistory.com/episodes/egypt/
Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bARxbJQpvWs
Published: 2026-07-02 · Length: 14 min

For five hundred years, Ancient Egypt wasn't a land of quiet tombs — it was the most powerful war machine on Earth, an empire whose chariots ran from deep in Sudan to the Euphrates. This is the complete rise and fall of Ancient Egypt: how the longest-lived empire in history conquered the ancient world, survived the catastrophe that ended the Bronze Age, and was finally beaten not by a stronger army — but by time itself.

Ancient Egypt explained — from the pyramids and the pharaohs to Hatshepsut, the battle of Megiddo, and Cleopatra, this is the story of the longest-lived civilization in human history: three thousand years of empire on the Nile, and how it finally fell to Rome. A military and social history of ancient Egyptian civilization: the pharaohs, the invasions it outlasted for three thousand years, and the archaeology that rebuilt its story.

Transcript:

You think you know Ancient Egypt. Pyramids. Golden masks. Dead kings sleeping under the sand. But for five

hundred years, Egypt was a war machine, chariots running from deep inside Sudan all the way to the Euphrates River, the most powerful empire on Earth.

And here's the part I can't get over: nothing stronger ever conquered it. In the end, Egypt was beaten by time itself. So how did the land of tombs become a conqueror, and then lose absolutely everything?

To understand the fall, you have to rewind. Way back.

Further than the pyramids. Egypt was not born an empire. It was born along a river. Picture a thin green ribbon of life snaking through a brutal desert. That is the Nile.

Around thirty-one hundred BC, by most reckonings, a king united the two halves of that ribbon. Upper Egypt in the south. Lower Egypt in the north. Tradition gives the credit to a king named Narmer. One crown.

One country. And the clock of pharaonic Egypt starts ticking.

Now here is the number that breaks your brain. That clock would run for roughly three thousand years. Cleopatra lived closer to the invention of the iPhone than to the building of the Great

Pyramid. Egypt was already ancient when Rome was a swamp. And those pyramids?

They came early. Shockingly early. The Old Kingdom, around twenty-six hundred BC, was the pyramid age. The three giants at Giza rose from the sand. The Great Pyramid was the tomb of a pharaoh named Khufu, built in roughly twenty-six years.

It stayed the tallest thing humans had ever made for thousands of years. But

think about that. By the time Egypt becomes a war machine, the pyramids are already a thousand years old. Even to the Egyptians, they

were ancient ruins. So what turned this calm river kingdom into a conqueror? The answer is humiliation. Roll forward to around sixteen fifty BC.

Foreign rulers seize the north. We call them the Hyksos. Outsiders, ruling the Delta from a city called Avaris. For the proud Egyptians, this was a wound that would not close. Their land.

Run by strangers. But the Hyksos brought something with them. The horse-drawn war chariot. The composite bow. Bronze weapons.

The Egyptians watched. The Egyptians learned. And then they turned those exact weapons

around. Around fifteen fifty BC, a pharaoh named Ahmose the First storms the Delta. He smashes Avaris and chases the Hyksos out of Egypt entirely.

And the moment he wins, something new is born. We call it the New Kingdom. The kingdom of tombs is about to become an empire of conquest. And

the first ruler to make that empire shine wasn't a king. It was a queen who became a king. Her name was Hatshepsut.

Around fourteen seventy-nine BC, she did the almost unthinkable. She took the full crown of pharaoh. Not queen.

Pharaoh. She wore the regalia of a king and ruled for roughly twenty-one years. And she didn't rule with war. She ruled with gold and

stone. She raised towering obelisks at Karnak. She carved a breathtaking temple into a cliff at Deir el-Bahari. She sent a famous trading fleet to a distant land called Punt. A golden age, built by a woman

who called herself king. So why have most people never heard of her? Here's the chilling part. After she died, someone tried to erase her.

Her name was chiseled off the monuments. Her face hacked away. Her statues smashed to pieces. And it almost worked. She was lost for thousands

of years, until Egyptologists rediscovered her in the eighteen-hundreds. But who

erased her, and why? For a long time, the finger pointed at the man who ruled next. The trouble is, we still aren't sure why it happened.

Some now think it was a cold political move to lock down the throne for the men who came after. We may never know. But we do know the man who came next. And he was the most dangerous pharaoh

Egypt ever produced. His name was Thutmose the Third. And historians gave him a nickname. The Napoleon of Egypt.

Over roughly twenty years, he launched around seventeen military campaigns. Year after year, marching out, conquering, returning. And his masterpiece came at a place called Megiddo,

around fourteen fifty-seven BC. Picture it. An enemy coalition is dug in. There are three roads to reach them.

Two are safe and wide. One is a narrow, terrifying mountain pass called the Aruna Pass, so tight the army has to march single file, one man behind another, helpless if

attacked. His generals beg him not to take it.

Thutmose takes it anyway. It's a gamble that should have gotten him slaughtered. Instead, he bursts out of that pass exactly where the enemy isn't looking. Total

surprise. The Egyptians shatter the Canaanite line. This, by the way, is the earliest battle in all of human history that we can reconstruct in real detail.

But here's the twist. Egypt almost threw it away. The soldiers stopped to grab the loot scattered across the battlefield instead of chasing the fleeing enemy.

The enemy escaped behind the city walls. And so a battle won in a single charge turned into a grinding siege that dragged on for around seven months. The

lesson the pharaohs never quite learned: greed can cost you the war.

When the dust settled, Egypt's power reached the Euphrates River in the north and deep into Nubia in the south. The edge of the

known world. Egypt was now the superpower of the ancient Near East. This was the peak. This was as high as it ever got. So

how do you fall from the top of the world? You start by fighting your own gods. Now here's the part nobody tells

you. The greatest threat to the Egyptian empire wasn't a foreign army. It was a single Egyptian king with an idea.

Around thirteen fifty-three BC, a pharaoh named Amenhotep the Fourth has a revolution in his head. He decides there is really only one god worth worshipping.

The sun-disk. The Aten. In his fifth year he renames himself Akhenaten, and he tries to switch off a thousand years of Egyptian religion overnight. Many call it the first known one-god religion in history. He goes

all in. He builds a brand-new capital city from nothing, out in the empty desert, dedicated entirely to the Aten. He closes the old temples.

He shuts down the old gods. And he yanks all that temple wealth, the immense fortune of the priesthood of Amun, straight back to the crown.

But while Akhenaten stares at his sun-god, the empire is burning. We know this because the letters survived. Clay tablets, dug out of his desert city, called the Amarna Letters. They are desperate cries for help from Egypt's allies

and vassals. One ruler, Rib-Hadda of the city of Byblos, sends plea after plea. Enemies are at his gates.

He begs for troops. And Egypt mostly ignores him. He sends dozens of letters. He loses his entire kingdom. The empire Thutmose built was being neglected to

death. So what happens when the revolutionary dies? Everything snaps back.

The throne passes to his young son, a boy of about nine.

We know that boy by another name. Tutankhamun. He abandons the desert capital. He restores the old gods. He moves the throne back to Thebes.

He even changes his own name, dropping the sun-god Aten and putting the old god Amun back in.

He was dead by about nineteen. And later pharaohs were so disgusted by the whole affair that they treated Akhenaten as a heretic, tore down his monuments, and struck his

name from the official king-lists. Erased. Just like Hatshepsut. Egypt survived its own revolution. Barely.

And then came the pharaoh who turned survival into the greatest PR campaign in history.

Ramesses the Second. Ramesses the Great. Around twelve seventy-four BC, he marches north to fight the Hittite Empire at a city called Kadesh. And he

walks straight into a trap. Enemy spies feed him false information. Overconfident, he pushes ahead with just his lead division, and the Hittites ambush

him. By the ancient accounts, they fielded around three thousand five hundred chariots. It was one of the biggest chariot battles ever fought.

And Ramesses is suddenly nearly alone, surrounded, fighting for his life, before a second division arrives just in time to save him. So what does Egypt's

greatest showman do? He goes home and covers the temple walls with carvings of his glorious, heroic, personal victory. The trouble is, it wasn't

really a victory. He never even captured the city of Kadesh. By the cold modern reading, the Battle of Kadesh was a draw.

But the real history happens about fifteen years later. Ramesses and the Hittite king sign a treaty, around twelve fifty-nine BC.

And it survives, in both the Egyptian and the Hittite versions. No more war. Mutual defense. The return of fugitives. It is the earliest surviving peace treaty in all of human history. Two superpowers, exhausted,

choosing peace in writing. That is the high-water mark of the ancient world.

And from a high-water mark, there is only one direction to go.

The first blow came from the sea. Around eleven seventy-five BC, under a pharaoh named Ramesses the Third, a wave of raiders we call the Sea Peoples crashes into Egypt

by land and by water. Who were they, exactly? Honestly, we still don't really know. Their origins are one of history's great unsolved mysteries.

But we know what they did. They were tearing the ancient world apart.

They burned the great city of Ugarit to the ground. They helped topple the entire Hittite Empire, the same superpower Egypt had just

made peace with. One by one, the great powers fell. We call it the Bronze Age collapse. And Egypt? Ramesses the Third beats the Sea Peoples on

land. Then he lures their fleet into the narrow branches of the Nile Delta and destroys it in the water. Egypt becomes

essentially the only great power of that age to survive the storm. But survival came at a terrible price. Egypt was alive, and gravely weakened.

And here's a strange little detail that tells you the empire was rotting from the inside.

Around eleven fifty-seven BC, the skilled workers who carved the royal tombs simply stopped

working. Their grain rations hadn't come. Egypt didn't run on coins, workers were paid in grain and beer.

They waited eighteen days past payday. Then they marched out and, by the record, chanted three words. "We are hungry." It's widely called the first

recorded labor strike in human history. The richest empire on Earth couldn't feed the men who built its tombs. It gets darker.

By the end of the New Kingdom, those very royal tombs were being robbed, sometimes by the officials sworn to guard them. The kings

weren't even safe in death. The priests had to gather up dozens of royal mummies, rewrap them, and hide them in secret caches. One cache, found

in eighteen eighty-one, held more than fifty kings and nobles stuffed into a single hidden tomb, Ahmose, Thutmose the Third, Ramesses the Great, all bundled together for safekeeping.

The conquerors of the world, hidden from their own people like contraband.

After that, Egypt simply came apart. Around ten seventy BC the unified empire shattered, kings in the north, priests of Amun ruling the south. And

then began the long humiliation. Around nine hundred forty-five BC, a dynasty of Libyan descent takes the throne. Then, around seven hundred

forty-seven BC, Nubian kings from the Kingdom of Kush, from what's now Sudan, march north

and conquer Egypt. And here's the twist: they revered it. They reunited the country and revived pyramid-building after a thousand years.

But the conquerors kept coming. The Assyrian Empire smashed the Kushite kings and, in six hundred sixty-three BC, sacked the holy southern city of Thebes, Egypt's sacred heart for over a thousand years.

Then, in five hundred twenty-five BC, the Persians under Cambyses swallowed Egypt whole. The age of native Egyptian kings was, for all practical purposes, over.

And then a young Macedonian named Alexander the Great took Egypt from the Persians in three hundred thirty-two BC. He founded a city on the coast and gave it his name. Alexandria.

After Alexander died, his general Ptolemy grabbed Egypt and started a Greek-speaking dynasty that ruled from that glittering city for nearly three centuries. The pharaohs of Egypt were now

Greeks. Which brings us, at last, to her. The most famous Egyptian

who ever lived. And she wasn't even Egyptian.

Cleopatra. The seventh of her name. Greek by blood, Macedonian descent, but unlike the rest of her family, she actually learned to speak the Egyptian language.

She was the last active ruler of Egypt. The last pharaoh.

And she made one bet to save her dying kingdom. Rome. She allied herself with the most powerful man in the world, Julius Caesar, and had his son. Then, after Caesar fell, she tied her fortunes

to the Roman general Mark Antony. It was a gamble for survival, Egypt clinging to Rome to stay alive. Remember Rome? The empire from before this one?

Here's where these two stories collide. In thirty-one BC, the Roman Octavian crushes Antony and Cleopatra's fleet at the Battle of Actium. Then he invades Egypt itself. Antony dies. And Cleopatra

dies too, in thirty BC, by legend, from the bite of a snake, though honestly, we don't know for sure how she died. And that was it. The last pharaoh

was gone. Octavian, soon to be called Augustus, annexed Egypt and turned it into a Roman province. He hunted down and executed Cleopatra's son.

And then he seized the real prize: Egypt's colossal supply of grain, which would now feed the city of Rome itself. The river kingdom

that fed itself for three thousand years now fed its conqueror.

Three thousand years. Older than almost anything we can name. An

empire that reached the Euphrates, survived the end of the Bronze Age, and outlived every rival of its time, finally swallowed by the same Rome we followed last time. The pyramids that opened

our story were already ancient ruins when the last pharaoh died beside them.

And maybe that's the real lesson hiding in the sand: even the longest-lived empire on Earth was, in the end, just

one more chapter for someone else's empire to inherit. Egypt didn't grow weak. It

just lasted long enough for the whole world to change around it, outliving every rival, every weapon, and every god it ever invented, until the only thing

left that could ever beat it was time. So which empire rises

next from the dust? Stick around, and we'll find out together.

---

## The Roman Empire Refused to Die

URL: https://doodlehistory.com/episodes/rome/
Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=R04KxCjiL7o
Published: 2026-06-24 · Length: 11 min

From two abandoned babies and a wolf to the most powerful empire the world had ever seen — and its long, strange fall. This is the complete story of Rome, hand-drawn and fact-checked: the founding myth, the Republic, Julius Caesar and the Rubicon, the first emperor Augustus, the golden age of the Pax Romana, the Colosseum and the eruption of Vesuvius, the crisis and the split, the sack of Rome, the last boy-emperor — and the legacy that still shapes your world today.

From the founding of Rome and the Roman Republic to the rise of the Caesars and the slow collapse of the Western Roman Empire, this is ancient Roman history explained simply — the conquests, the emperors, the corruption, and the single weakness that brought the greatest empire of the ancient world to its knees. A military history of ancient Rome: the legions and civil wars, the sack of 476, and the Roman state that survived in the East for another thousand years.
